title: iOS 27: Here are Apple’s full release notes
snippet: Today Apple announced that iOS 27 will launch next Monday, September 14. Here are the full release notes for the major new iPhone update. more…
fullText:
Today Apple announced that iOS 27 will launch next Monday, September 14. Here are the full release notes for the major new iPhone update.

Apple’s official iOS 27 release notes available now

Apple has published the full iOS 27 release notes as part of its RC update today. They’re included unedited below:

Siri AI (All iPhone 16 models and later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max)

A more capable and conversational version of Siri is rolling out to users. It helps you find what you need and get more done, drawing on capabilities like personal context understanding, app actions, onscreen awareness, and access to broad world knowledge

New voice experience offers more expressive and natural-sounding voices, and lets you customize expressivity and pace to make Siri more personal to you using powerful on-device models on iPhone Air and iPhone 17 Pro models and later

Dedicated Siri app provides an easy way to revisit an existing conversation or kick off a new one, and privately syncs conversations across your Apple products with iCloud

Siri mode in Camera integrates Visual Intelligence into the Camera app, letting you ask questions and take action with what’s in front of you, like splitting a bill or looking up nutritional info for a plate of food

Write with Siri enables you to generate a draft from scratch, edit what you’ve written, or get feedback from Siri virtually anywhere you type. In Messages & Mail, Siri personalizes your writing style based on your relationships, and uses unique phrases and punctuation that you’ve previously used in your conversations with those people

Apple Intelligence across apps (All iPhone 16 models and later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max)

Photos

Spatial Reframing lets you adjust the composition of a photo after it was taken by virtually changing the camera position

Extend tool intelligently expands images beyond their edges with realistic infill, so you can straighten horizons, change aspect ratios, or add more space around a subject

Clean Up supports removing even larger objects, with more realistic, high-quality results, and you can choose between Fast mode for small blemishes or High Quality for more intricate edits

Safari

Organize by Topic uses Apple Intelligence to sort your tabs, analyzing webpages and automatically grouping similar tabs together

Notify Me can periodically check a webpage for updates, like price changes and item availability

Describe an Extension lets you create a custom extension using natural language to adjust your view of a website’s content or formatting

All-new Image Playground uses a new generative model to make high-quality images in virtually any style, including photorealistic, lets you modify your images using touch and natural language, and lets you generate Lock Screen wallpapers and Contact Posters with personalized suggestions

Describe a Shortcut lets you use natural language to create a shortcut or refine an existing one

Home

Summarized activity notifications combine related alerts across accessories into a single notification

Video descriptions for HomeKit Secure Video recordings summarize what’s happening in a clip for eligible iCloud+ subscribers

Camera clip search lets you find specific moments from your HomeKit Secure Video cameras by searching in the Home app or Spotlight when on an eligible iCloud+ plan

Describe an event in Calendar lets you use natural language to create an event, and details like the time, location, invitees, and event title are filled in using Apple Intelligence

Suggestions in Mail help you take action based on the context of your emails, like getting directions to a restaurant you booked

Call Context in the Phone app understands when you’re speaking to certain businesses and proactively surfaces relevant information from across your apps, like a confirmation code or a reservation number

Accessibility

VoiceOver enhancements include more detailed and contextual image understanding for photos, charts, and screenshots, a conversational experience that lets you ask questions about your screen or surroundings, and a new way to get answers fast with an Action button integration

An enhanced Magnifier experience offers conversational visual assistance for users with low vision, with a high-contrast interface and natural language app controls for zooming and other Magnifier functions

A smarter Accessibility Reader uses intelligence to provide better text cleanup and formatting, images and tables, on-demand summaries, and translation

Voice Control flexible inputs help you navigate your device with just your voice by describing elements on screen in your own words, like “tap the gear” or “tap the button in the top right”

And more, including additional ways to create and modify Genmoji, automatic proofreading, and more accurate dictation using an on-device model on iPhone Air and iPhone 17 Pro models and later

Child Safety

Improved setup experience for new child accounts lets parents choose the exact apps their kids can access when they set up an iPhone for their child

Ask to Browse gives parents the option to approve each new website before their child can view it

Expanded Communication Safety protections help intervene before children see gore or violent content in shared images and videos

Time Allowances help parents set boundaries around how long kids can use apps across Entertainment, Games, and Social Media apps, offering guidance based on expert research and tailored to each child’s age

Schedules let parents choose which apps their kids can access at different points in their day and across weekdays and weekends

Redesigned Screen Time settings give parents at-a-glance information about how their kids use their devices, and controls to adjust access in just a few taps

System Improvements

Liquid Glass refinements improve overall readability, and a new slider in Settings lets you personalize its appearance from ultra-clear to fully tinted

title: Apple Didn’t Make a New iPhone Air This Year. This May Be Why
snippet: More affordable options, like a possible iPhone Air 2, were not on Apple’s 2026 roster.
fullText:
We got a host of new iPhones at Wednesday’s Apple Surprise and Shine event. But there were some noticeable absences: base iPhone 18 models, as Apple focused purely on premium devices, and a second iteration of its lightweight iPhone Air.

At just 5.6mm thick and weighing only 165 grams, last year’s $999 iPhone 17 Air gave buyers a middle-ground option between the base iPhone 17 and the iPhone 17 Pro models, and for a pretty reasonable price. 

While sales of the iPhone Air were reportedly disappointing, it was arguably a first step toward launching the iPhone Duo — a demonstration that a slim, lightweight phone could be just as durable and high-functioning as a fully specced-out one. It came with just one rear 48-megapixel wide-angle camera, a smaller battery and a single speaker.

The Air’s pared-back features and slim profile would have been pivotal to designing Apple’s new folding phone, since foldables must be both slim and make similar compromises on specs — the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 only has two rear lenses, compared with the three that come on other Galaxy models, and the iPhone Duo likewise has just two rear cameras.

We were hoping Apple would release another version of the Air with improved cameras and battery life, especially since that middle ground still exists. Some people just want a phone that’s slightly better than the base iPhone, and many people want a capable phone without having to spend upward of $1,199 — the cheapest phone Apple announced on Wednesday as it took the wraps off premium handsets like the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.

	

			

	

			

									

						iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max					

							

		

Many people also don’t want a phone that folds. CNET’s survey of more than 2,600 adults last month found that 75% were not interested in a foldable iPhone and that most would want to spend less than $1,000 if they did get one. But the Duo costs between $1,999 and $3,199 — far exceeding the iPhone Air’s original $999 price tag.

Apple also raised the prices on its iPhone 17 lineup on Wednesday as it announced its new high-end handsets, leaving the middle ground with fewer options, even in previously available models. The iPhone 17 Air now starts at $1,099, with the price increases coming amid RAMageddon, the global memory shortage caused by the spike in AI tools. Apple continues to whittle down options for more budget-conscious consumers in a difficult economy. 

We’re still holding out hope that the iPhone 18 Air has been pushed back until a rumored spring launch, where it could be unveiled alongside an iPhone 18 base model and a potential iPhone 18E, the budget follow-up to this year’s iPhone 17E. 

IDC Worldwide Device Trackers Senior Research Director Nabila Popal likewise believes Apple is strategically withholding the second iPhone Air until next year to bundle with the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18E — launching a trio of more affordable smartphones to contrast with the premium trio of the iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max and Duo that were just announced.

“It allows Apple to spread its shipments more evenly throughout the year and simultaneously allow the spotlight on the premium models this fall — especially the new iPhone foldable,” Popal said. “Apple is spreading its portfolio to a wider consumer demographic and giving consumers more choice.”

But for now, the lack of lower-end models means anyone wanting to upgrade their phone to a brand-new Apple handset will be stuck choosing between an $1,199 iPhone 18 Pro and up to an eye-watering $3,199 for a 2TB iPhone Duo.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Corinne Reichert
						

						

							Senior Editor

She holds degrees in law and communications, and currently writes news, analysis and features for CNET across the topics of electric vehicles, broadband networks, mobile devices, big tech, artificial intelligence, home technology and entertainment. In her spare time, she watches soccer games and F1 races, and goes to Disneyland as often as possible.

title: Where’s the iPhone 18? Here’s Why Apple Didn’t Reveal a New Standard iPhone
snippet: We saw the iPhone 18 Pro and foldable iPhone Duo launch, but the baseline model may be coming next year — presumably for a few big reasons.
fullText:
Without a new iPhone 18, Apple has kept the iPhone 17 as its main baseline phone in its lineup — though with a price bump.

																			Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET
												
			
				

Apple revealed a new lineup of premium devices at its Sept. 9 event, including new Apple Watches, the new iPhone 18 Pro and the first foldable iPhone Duo, with one glaring omission: The standard iPhone 18 was nowhere to be seen. Apple didn’t even mention the missing phone, but rumors suggest it will launch early in 2027 — and there are several reasons why the company would delay its entry-level model to next year.

It’s a pivotal moment for Apple. The event was the first for new CEO John Ternus, who started his role on Sept. 1, and we’re learning in real time whether he plans to stay the course his predecessor, Tim Cook, set or take Apple in a different direction. The foldable iPhone Duo is a bold foray into a niche subset of phones that sell a fraction of the flat iPhones that make up the bulk of Apple’s earnings every quarter. 

But Apple has masterfully navigated expanding its lineup with a product that fits between its existing devices. The iPad was introduced to fit the niche between phones and laptops, and the foldable iPhone seems aimed at the gap between smartphone and iPad. In the background is the RAM shortage, making memory and components pricier than ever — and indeed, the iPhone 18 Pro got a $100 price bump over its predecessors, and the current iPhone 17 got more expensive as well.

The iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable, automatically adjusts its display to its orientation.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Amid those conditions, there are potential reasons for Apple to push its more basic phones to next year. The easiest assumption is that it will make the company more money, with the iPhone 18 Pro undoubtedly priced higher than the iPhone 18 — anyone eager to upgrade right now only has the more expensive phones to choose from. 

It’s possible that Apple wants to space out its different models to better meet demand, possibly accounting for the production complications that arise with parts getting pricier from the RAM shortage. Or maybe they just want to give the folding iPhone Ultra the limelight. Nabila Popal, senior research director at the International Data Corporation, feels this move is brilliant strategy and surprisingly not spurred by the memory crises or supply side constraints.

“It allows Apple to spread its shipments more evenly throughout the year and simultaneously allow the spotlight on the premium models this fall — especially the new iPhone foldable,” Popal said.

Releasing the iPhone 18 later may not dim the unit’s sales, either: In the first half of 2024 and 2025, the baseline iPhones released the fall before still made up 16% of Apple’s total shipments in those periods, Popal said.

One thing is for sure: Apple is making big shifts with its Sept. 9 event; its tagline, Surprise and Shine, is telling.

The iPhone Air (mostly) survived my unhinged screen time. 

Jesse Orrall/Zooey Liao/CNET

A lineup shakeup: Bumping the iPhone 18 to 2027 and no iPhone Air 2

Last year’s iPhone Air was a marvel of engineering, following what seemed to be a new trend of slim phones after the Samsung Galaxy S25 Edge released earlier in 2025. But what had been a trend has disappeared in 2026, with no high-profile phones released whose main claim to fame is an extremely slender width.

Presumably, that’s because Apple and Samsung lost confidence after the very low sales for either slim phone. The IDC reported that the iPhone Air sold just 7.7 million units over four quarters, and the Galaxy S25 Edge sold 2.3 million over five quarters. Neither phone exceeded 1.8% of total phone sales for either brand across those time periods, IDC said. It’s always possible that Apple does release another iPhone Air later on.

But all the work to slim down conventional phones seemingly hasn’t gone to waste — it’s likely contributed to trimming the width on foldable phones. The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold is 5 millimeters when unfolded flat, but Samsung has gone even further, with the wide-format Galaxy Z Fold 8 down to 4.5mm and the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra reaching 4.1mm when fully unfolded. Considering that the Galaxy S25 Edge was 5.8mm, the company’s best foldables reaching nearly 2mm thinner is an achievement.

So Apple is relegating its iPhone 18 to 2027, likely earlier in the year. That’s around when it launched the iPhone 17E (in March 2026), so the company could be bundling its baseline iPhone 18 and likely even cheaper iPhone 18E in the same event. This would set a new schedule for Apple: more affordable phones earlier in spring, and then the next generation of its top-tier premium iPhones in its typical September launch window. This gives each lineup its own well-deserved attention and spotlight, IDC’s Popal noted.

“Apple is spreading its portfolio to a wider consumer demographic and giving consumers more choice, which is always good for business,” Popal said.

The iPhone 18 could be accompanied by an iPhone 18E and even an iPhone Air 2, Popal predicts. Even if these will conceivably be cheaper than the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo models, they’ll still likely be pricier than their predecessors — because Apple’s already made its older iPhones more expensive.

Typically, when Apple announces a new standard iPhone, the previous version is discounted $100 and sold for another year or so. Instead, it’s raised iPhone 17‘s price at $900, ripping the band-aid off now before the next baseline iPhone launches at a higher price. This could better distinguish it from the traditionally cheaper E-series phones like the $600 iPhone 17E, which appeal to a different, more budget-conscious segment of the market, Popal believes. Apple knows consumers will feel the sticker shock of the price increases, which is why it’s retained the iPhone 16 in its current lineup — though it, too, has gotten a bump back up to its original $800 price, a change from the discounted $700 it had been up until this morning.

That twice-per-year release schedule matches what Samsung has done for years, with an event in January for its premium flat phones and then another in August for its foldables. We’ll have to see whether Apple turns its spring showcase into an announcement event — perhaps bundling it with the Macs and home accessories that have sometimes simply launched via press release. It’s a brand new day for Apple, and anything is possible under Ternus. We’ll just have to see what’s in store for iPhones, folding and flat.

title: iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone 17 Pro: Here’s everything new
snippet: Today Apple unveiled iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, its latest flagship models. Here’s everything new with iPhone 18 Pro vs last year’s iPhone 17 Pro. more…
fullText:
Today Apple unveiled iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, its latest flagship models. Here’s everything new with iPhone 18 Pro vs last year’s iPhone 17 Pro.

Cameras: New 48MP Main camera with variable aperture

Every year Apple makes the iPhone camera system better. But with four different cameras on the iPhone Pro models, sometimes changes are limited to one camera or another. Last year, for example, brought an all-new Center Stage front camera and Telephoto improvements.

With iPhone 18 Pro, the Main camera is the focus of Apple’s upgrades.

Apple says the 48MP Fusion Main camera is all-new, notably adding a variable aperture feature. Here are the details:

The new 48MP Fusion Main camera with variable aperture is the most advanced camera Apple has ever made, bringing aperture control to iPhone for the first time along with even more creative control. Six laser-cut blades smoothly transition between different apertures, making it incredibly easy to capture the best shot by automatically adjusting for depth of field and lighting. Combined with a new sensor that improves image quality, the result is better low-light photography, crisper detail in the back of group photos, and more unique shots. Variable aperture also provides more control for creative pros by giving them the ability to manually adjust any of the four aperture settings in the Camera app, and an API is available to developers for even more control across the aperture range in their apps.

Users will be able to switch between ƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8, and ƒ/4.0 variable aperture options.

Apple also introduced a variety of new Camera app software features, including updated Photographic Styles and pro controls for lens aperture, shutter speed, white balance, and viewing histogram. Those are all exclusive to iPhone 18 Pro too, as are Smart focus tracking, Cinematic mode effects from video, and Apple Reference Image.

Performance: A20 Pro chip and thermal upgrades

The new A20 Pro chip is a big upgrade over last year’s A19 Pro. That’s partly thanks to the new 2nm process it was built on, which improves performance and efficiency.

A20 Pro has a 6-core CPU, with 2 new super cores that Apple says are the fastest in any smartphone, plus 4 new efficiency cores. There’s also a 7-core GPU with 40% faster graphics performance, increased bandwidth, and faster Neural Accelerators than A19 Pro.

iOS 27 is packed with major AI features, and A20 Pro is an especially big leap for AI. That’s thanks to a new Dual 16-core Neural Engine—that’s double the number of cores as A19 Pro.

Finally, A20 Pro has a 50% increase in memory bandwidth, and thermal performance is improved thanks to a second-generation vapor chamber. Ultimately, these changes lead to 40% improved sustained performance over iPhone 17 Pro.

Design: New colors, uniform rear design, redesigned Dynamic Island

iPhone 18 Pro largely retains the same design as iPhone 17 Pro, with a prominent camera plateau on the back.

The most notable design change involves color. iPhone 18 Pro comes in four new colors: Burgundy, Glacier, Black, and Silver. This gives it a fresh look versus the bold iPhone 17 Pro colors.

Apple has also updated the back of iPhone 18 Pro with a more unified blend of colors between the glass cutout and aluminum frame. Last year’s models had a two-tone design, but this year it’s a more uniform look.

Finally, there’s a redesigned Dynamic Island on the front of iPhone 18 Pro. Its smaller footprint enables up to three simultaneous Live Activities.

Battery: Best-ever battery life, faster charging

iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max offered the best-ever iPhone battery life. But this year Apple is upping battery life yet again, with big gains especially for iPhone 18 Pro Max.

up to 36 hours

up to 33 hours

Faster wired charging is included with iPhone 18 Pro too, which can get 50% charge in just 15 minutes.

Connectivity: Apple-designed C2 modem on at least 18 Pro

Apple has a new in-house C2 modem debuting in iPhone 18 Pro. It replaces the Qualcomm modem found in iPhone 17 Pro, while still including support for mmWave in the US.

Here are the details via Apple’s press release:

iPhone 18 Pro introduces C2, Apple’s next-generation cellular modem system, which brings AI-powered improvements to cellular quality and reliability. C2 delivers meaningfully faster uploads when compared to C1X while consuming 15 percent less energy, and now supports mmWave in the U.S.

Interestingly, Apple’s tech specs page suggests that C2 might be exclusive to iPhone 18 Pro, with the Pro Max model sticking with Qualcomm.

iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone 17 Pro: wrap-up

	

iPhone 18 Pro starts at a higher $1,199 price, compared to $1,099 for iPhone 17 Pro. iPhone 18 Pro Max gets a similar $100 increase, starting at $1,299.

title: iPhone 17, iPhone Air, and iPhone 17e just got more expensive

fullText:
With the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max now starting $100 more than their predecessors, Apple has also applied the price hike to the entire iPhone lineup, including the phones that didn’t change at all.

That means the base model iPhone 17 now starts at $899, up from $799. Similarly, the iPhone Air breaks into the four digit club, now priced at $1099 to start.

The same $100 price bumps also applies to iPhone 17e, and iPhone 16. The iPhone 17e is now $699, up from its previous $599 floor. 

Of course, people may balk at the fact that the same iPhone models that have been on sale for a year already are now more expensive without any changes. 

But Apple is continuing to react to changing market conditions when it comes to rising component pricing like RAM and storage, and ‘only’ a $100 jump is less than some analysts had been predicting.

title: No iPhone 18 announced today: Here’s why
snippet: Today at its September event, Apple unveiled iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, but there was no base model iPhone 18 introduced. Here’s why. more…
fullText:
Today at its September event, Apple unveiled iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, but there was no base model iPhone 18 introduced. Here’s why.

iPhone 18 base model expected to launch in early 2027, as Apple shifts release schedule

Normally, it might be common to refer to today’s Apple event as the “iPhone 18 event.”

But in a move that likely surprised many, Apple didn’t announce an iPhone 18 today—at least not the base model.

Instead, the company debuted three high-end new iPhones only: iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo.

This flagship lineup differs significantly from Apple’s prior pattern of shipping a new base iPhone at the same time as Pro models. But reporting dating all the way back to May 2025 predicted such a change was coming.

Per widespread reports, Apple’s three new iPhone models introduced today will be joined by three more debuts in early 2027:

iPhone 18

iPhone 18e

iPhone Air 2

So the base iPhone 18 hasn’t been canceled, it’s just shipping later than usual.

Why the change?

One theory is that since Apple wants to expand the iPhone lineup more than ever, with new models like the foldable Duo, it didn’t want to overcrowd the fall. Thus, splitting major iPhone launches into fall and spring cycles might be advantageous.

Another possible reason is that Apple saw the current memory shortage coming, and knew it would be a struggle to meet demand if it launched the base iPhone 18 at the same time as Pro and Duo models.

In any case, the iPhone 18 is still coming—just not until the early months of 2027.

title: Hands-on: Nothing’s $25 CMF Buds Neo are way better than the price suggests
snippet: Last month, Nothing’s CMF brand launched a new pair of $25 earbuds in the CMF Buds Neo. Too good to be true, I figured, but after getting my hands on them, I’m pleasantly surprised by what they bring to the table despite some expected downsides. more…
fullText:
Last month, Nothing’s CMF brand launched a new pair of $25 earbuds in the CMF Buds Neo. Too good to be true, I figured, but after getting my hands on them, I’m pleasantly surprised by what they bring to the table despite some expected downsides.

The CMF Buds Neo bring a lot to the table on paper. 52-hour battery life, active noise cancellation, some flashy colors, and even dual-device connections alongside support for the Nothing X app and EQ presets. For $25, it’s a compelling package. 

How does it deliver in real life?

I’ve spent a few hours listening to CMF Buds Neo and, honestly, I’m pretty impressed!

	

At their core, they get the job done. The earbuds have decent sound quality, though they’re a bit hollow on default settings. I found that turning down the bass enhancement improves the sound quality, and they’re more optimized for speech (podcasts, etc) than music. Nothing Ear (3a) sound far better; don’t get me wrong, but probably not 4x better as the price on paper suggests.

The sound quality is the most important thing here when the price is so low, and it’s certainly more than good enough to make these a good deal. And there’s clearly more weight put in the price than anything else. CMF Buds Neo have some clear and obvious downsides. The case is cheap-feeling despite looking very nice, and the same goes for the earbuds – the materials feel cheap, but they fit nice in my ear and stay comfortable over a few hours of use. The touchpads on the earbuds are responsive, but lack a play/pause gesture by default. Another downside is the range, as I found these disconnect from my Fold 8 more quickly than other earbuds I’ve tested in recent memory. The case magnets that hold the earbuds in place work well, and there are some nice touches such as a snappy hinge and the lanyard hole on a rotating corner piece. 

There’s also no pairing button on the case, something that will never fail to annoy me, but at least there’s Google Fast Pair – humorously, the Fast Pair pop-up lacks a picture of the earbuds and just says “blue” on the variant I bought.

Downsides are aplenty here, which really shouldn’t come as a surprise. But, at the core, you’re getting earbuds that sound good enough, have most important features, and cost just $25. If you need a spare pair of earbuds to throw in a backpack or at your bedside, or a daily driver on a budget, these are a winner in my book.

title: Gemini app makes Daily Brief free in the US

fullText:
After introducing at I/O 2026 in May, Google is making Daily Brief in the Gemini app available for free in the US.

Daily Brief generates a list of your to-dos and priorities every morning. Gemini uses Personal Intelligence to look at your Gmail, Google Calendar, and other Connected Apps, as well as past Gemini chats.

The Daily Brief starts with a “Top of mind” section that shows “timely, actionable items,” such as tasks with upcoming deadlines. “FYI” will show other items that have dates attached. “Looking ahead” is the final section with a focus on long-term goals and “suggested next steps to help you achieve them.”

You can tap on items to “Mark complete” or start a “Chat” with Gemini. There’s also the ability to leave “Helpful” or “Not helpful” feedback.

	

Example use cases include:

For students: Manage class schedules, organize study plans, and track applications.

For entrepreneurs: Surface actionable client emails and update task reminders.

For parents: Manage school communications, track family milestones, and handle household tasks.

For job seekers: Quickly act on recruiter inquiries, prepare for interviews, and monitor application statuses.

As of last Friday, Gemini Daily Brief no longer requires a Google AI subscription in the US. It’s available to personal Google Accounts with Personal Intelligence, Memory, and the Google Workspace integration enabled.

You can access it from the Gemini side panel, with Google also sending a notification every morning. You can disable that alert by going to the account menu and configuring “Notifications.” 

Another way to interact with the digest is through Gemini Live: “What’s my daily brief?”

iPhone 18 Pro is about to be unveiled, and due to a lineup overhaul this year, it’s set to become Apple’s new default model like never before.

Apple has offered multiple new iPhone models every year for a very long time. And no doubt will for many years to come.

But at this week’s Apple event, a big shakeup is coming to the iPhone lineup.

iPhone 18 Pro Max

iPhone Ultra

By delaying iPhone 18 beyond its typical release schedule, iPhone 18 Pro will essentially become Apple’s new default model.

Users who need a cheaper device will still be able to choose from last year’s iPhone 17, or the iPhone 17e or iPhone Air. But in all the marketing we see from Apple and carrier partners this fall and into the holidays, there will be no ‘iPhone 18’ to promote as the new default. Instead, iPhone 18 Pro will fill that role.

iPhone Ultra will be too expensive, and likely fairly niche in comparison.

So for the average person who wants “the new iPhone,” Apple will basically have just two options: iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max.

It’s an interesting experiment, and could see iPhone 18 Pro become the new bestselling Pro model. But paired with expected price increases, it’s also a risk for Apple. Prospective upgraders might hold on to their current iPhone longer because there’s no iPhone 18 to upgrade to.

title: Arizona’s lifeline for chip manufacturing is drying up
snippet: Water intake towers at the Hoover Dam stand next to a bleached "bathtub ring" on the banks of Lake Mead on September 1st in Lake Mead National Recreation Area, Arizona. The reservoir has hit historic lows as the Colorado River experiences unprecedented drought. | Photo: Getty Images Arizona, an epicenter for the bipartisan push to revive American chip manufacturing, is about to lose more than a quarter of the water it typically pulls each year from the Colorado River. The 1,400-mile waterway is a crucial lifeline for the region and other western states. A recent federal decision on how to manage its dwindling flow hits Arizona, and its already drought-prone desert communities, particularly hard. The river provides more than a third of the Grand Canyon State's water. Arizona has been a manufacturing hub since the start of the semiconductor industry, and now it's where TSMC and Intel are expanding massive factories to m … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
The 1,400-mile waterway is a crucial lifeline for the region and other western states. A recent federal decision on how to manage its dwindling flow hits Arizona, and its already drought-prone desert communities, particularly hard. The river provides more than a third of the Grand Canyon State’s water. Arizona has been a manufacturing hub since the start of the semiconductor industry, and now it’s where TSMC and Intel are expanding massive factories to make advanced chips for AI — a water-intensive effort.

City planners and industry leaders have already taken precautions to conserve water and find alternative sources. It’s a resource that is likely to become more expensive for manufacturers and residents alike as they learn to rely less on the Colorado River. That’s already raising tensions over who shoulders the costs for new infrastructure needed to adapt, as well as what constitutes a good use of water. The challenges that come with managing a limited water supply are only going to grow as AI demands a larger share.

TSMC and Intel are expanding massive factories to make advanced chips for AI — a water intensive effort

“Our economy is changing, and that’s really painful,” says Kathryn Sorensen, research director at the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University. “When there’s a water scarcity issue you have to start looking at what the uses of that water are that bring the most value to the community.”

Agriculture has been a major part of Arizona’s economy since it became a state, and still gobbles up more than 70 percent of the state’s water. Industrial uses, including the chip manufacturing that’s had a foothold in the state since the 1940s, account for just 6 percent.

While the amount of water that semiconductor factories, or fabs, use is still quite small compared to agriculture, the chip industry is growing fast. Fabs use “ultra-pure” water to clean surfaces and etch sensitive chips. It takes more municipal water to create a smaller amount of ultra-pure water through deionization and reverse osmosis. A typical facility might use 10 million gallons of ultra-pure water a day, which could require up to 16 million gallons of municipal water.

New chip factories are sprouting up in Arizona’s desert with the help of federal funding. President Joe Biden signed the ​​CHIPS and Science Act into law in 2022, setting aside $52.7 billion to expand domestic chip manufacturing. Armed with a $7.86 billion grant from the government, Intel is planning to spend $32 billion on two new factories and an expansion of an existing facility in Arizona. In 2025, the company’s facilities in Chandler, Arizona withdrew more than 2.7 billion gallons of freshwater, according to its latest corporate responsibility report.

TSMC, the world’s largest chipmaker, received up to $6.6 billion in CHIPS Act funding and decided to build at least six new semiconductor fabs in Phoenix. TSMC’s first fab in Arizona uses roughly 4.75 million gallons of water a day, the company told The Verge last year. It’s approximately equivalent to the water usage of more than 14,000 homes a day, or 2 percent of Phoenix’s housing. That amount grows with each new fab the company builds, and with the more advanced manufacturing processes TSMC is developing. The company recycles 65 percent of the water it uses in Arizona, TSMC says, a figure that’s supposed to grow to at least 90 percent when it finishes building a water reclamation plant.

“There’s not enough water for everything we want to do with it.”

The Colorado River is the state’s biggest renewable source of water. But the Colorado River Basin has faced “unprecedented” drought for more than a quarter century, according to the US Bureau of Reclamation. Climate change, unfortunately, is also making the region more dry as growing water demand adds to decades of overuse.

“There’s not enough water for everything we want to do with it,” Sorensen, who previously worked as the director of Phoenix Water Services, says. “So what do we have enough water for? What are the uses we most value? Is it cotton or is it microchips?”

With 40 million Americans from Denver to Los Angeles relying on water from the Colorado River, states have been tussling over how to allocate the remaining water for years. Guidelines for how to manage that water, collectively known as the “Law of the River,” expire this year. After states failed to reach an agreement on their own, the US Department of the Interior finalized its own plan in August for how to move forward. It outlines steep cuts for downriver states: Arizona, Nevada, and California. Arizona stands to lose the most, at least 760,000 acre-feet of water a year starting in 2027. An acre-foot represents how much water it would take to cover an acre with a foot of water, and is enough to supply about three homes with water for a year in the Phoenix area. The City of Phoenix uses about 300,000 acre feet of water in a year.

Maricopa County, home to Intel and TSMC’s chip fabs, isn’t as reliant on water from the Colorado River as other counties. Its primary resource is groundwater, but surface water flowing from the Colorado and Salt rivers still make up close to 40 percent of the county’s supply.

Local leaders insist that Phoenix and other cities in the region are prepared for water cuts, citing plans to make up for the shortfall with underground water stores and other surface water sources. “For the most part, they’ve planned accordingly and can fall back onto water that was previously stored underground,” Sorensen says.

But even without sudden tap water shortages, Sorensen expects utility bills to climb over time. The transition to alternative water resources will entail new infrastructure, like new wells and pipes. That’s likely to be the most significant driver of higher tap water prices, Sorensen explains.

Meanwhile, the city of Phoenix is pushing back, with Mayor Kate Gallego arguing that the federal government’s decision to cut the state’s intake “does not provide the fair, basin-wide leadership the Colorado River crisis demands.” That said, “Phoenix is prepared for this moment because of decades of planning and conservation, we will push for new federal support to mitigate the rising cost of water that will result from this federal decision,” Gallego added in an August press release. A spokesperson for the city declined to comment further in an interview.

TSMC in particular, located in Phoenix, will be subject to the same price hikes as its neighbors. Phoenix is unique in that it sets the same water rates for companies as it does for residential customers. Cities often charge industrial customers less if they want to attract certain businesses.

“The cost of water will increase for TSMC,” Sorensen says. “Everyone pays the same rate for water in the city of Phoenix, whether you’re a mom-and-pop store, a family of eight, or TSMC.”

TSMC and Intel declined interviews with The Verge for this story. Both have made public commitments, however, to minimize the amount of fresh water they consume.

“A stable supply of water is critical to chip production,” TSMC deputy spokesperson Nina Kao said in an emailed statement. “One of the reasons the city of Phoenix was selected for our US expansion is because of their long-term water plan, which includes varied water supply sources, as well as steps taken in preparation for reduced water supplies over the course of decades.”

Apprehensions are still mounting over the impact that AI and the tech industry as a whole have on the region. AI has spawned a new generation of semiconductor factories, chip packaging plants, and data centers across Arizona.

“A stable supply of water is critical to chip production.”

“It’s almost happening at a level that’s difficult to wrap your head around,” says Jennifer Martin-McLeod, a program manager for the Grand Canyon chapter of Sierra Club. “To try to say ‘Everybody take a breath and think through what we’re doing’ is difficult when you have that steamroller of money coming at your state to try to make it all happen overnight.”

She has broader concerns about the health of the Colorado River and wildlife that depends on it. Over the long term, Sorensen points out that a shortage of water from the Colorado River will result in the depletion of groundwater in Central Arizona, as most cities cope by increasing how much water they draw from local aquifers. “It’s something they can sustain, but it is only sustained at a cost to future generations,” she adds.

The impact of water cuts next year will be felt most by typical residents, Martin-McLeod says. “For me, that’s going to mean serious lifestyle changes. … But to an enormous chip manufacturer, that’s maybe just part of the cost of doing business, you know?”

The 1,400-mile waterway is a crucial lifeline for the region and other western states. A recent federal decision on how to manage its dwindling flow hits Arizona, and its already drought-prone desert communities, particularly hard. The river provides more than a third of the Grand Canyon State’s water. Arizona has been a manufacturing hub since the start of the semiconductor industry, and now it’s where TSMC and Intel are expanding massive factories to make advanced chips for AI — a water-intensive effort.

City planners and industry leaders have already taken precautions to conserve water and find alternative sources. It’s a resource that is likely to become more expensive for manufacturers and residents alike as they learn to rely less on the Colorado River. That’s already raising tensions over who shoulders the costs for new infrastructure needed to adapt, as well as what constitutes a good use of water. The challenges that come with managing a limited water supply are only going to grow as AI demands a larger share.

fullText:
A new feature coming to Slack will allow you to build interactive reports, polls, dashboards, presentations, microsites, and other tools directly inside a chat. With Slackforce Surfaces, you can describe to Slackbot what you need, and it will use AI to gather information from relevant conversations and connected apps, like Google Drive or Salesforce, to create it.

Once Slackbot creates a Surface, you can share it with colleagues and pin it to channels, allowing other people to view it, interact with it, and leave comments. In one example shared by Slack, a user asks Slackbot for help creating an arcade-themed visualization of AI token usage. The AI assistant then generates an interactive dashboard showing token usage across different divisions, such as sales, design, and engineering.

“You’re not exporting your data to some other tool to make sense of it, you’re asking Slackbot to build the dashboard, the deck, the report right where the conversation already is, and your whole team can act on it together,” Ryan Gavin, Slack’s chief marketing officer, tells The Verge in an email.

This update comes just months after Slack overhauled Slackbot to make the tool more like an AI assistant, allowing it to summarize information across channels, sort through messages, and find time to schedule meetings. It also added collaborative vibe coding channels last month.

It seems like there are many other ways to use Surfaces, too, like building a live dashboard for a customer support queue that other workers can view, or creating a weather-themed financial forecast that pulls in data from connected apps. Slack notes that the feature will only pull information that you’ve given its AI tools permission to access.

Slackforce Surfaces is available to all customers — including those who use it for free — with Slackbot enabled in their workspace. You’ll be able to use it with live data starting in October.

title: YouTube details NFL Sunday Ticket pricing & availability for 2026 season, including a 50% discount
snippet: YouTube is starting its fourth season as the home of NFL Sunday Ticket and, ahead of Week 1 games, an overview of availability and pricing has been detailed, including a big discount for new customers. more…
fullText:
YouTube is starting its fourth season as the home of NFL Sunday Ticket and, ahead of Week 1 games, an overview of availability and pricing has been detailed, including a big discount for new customers.

For the 2026-2027 season, NFL Sunday Ticket on YouTube TV will start at $240/year.

That’s thanks to a big discount YouTube is running, but it’s only available for new subscribers. For those eligible, it’s a discount of up to 50%. For existing customers, the costs are $378/year through YouTube TV (in addition to monthly subscription costs) or $480/year through YouTube Primetime Channels.

You can sign up via YouTube’s Sunday Ticket website.

	

NFL Sunday Ticket packages at YouTube

On a support page and through a thread on Reddit, Google details what games are and are not available through NFL Sunday Ticket on YouTube this year, and where you can watch those other games.

It breaks down to:

Thursday Night Football: Not available on YouTube/YouTube TV

Sunday Afternoon Games: Out-of-market via Sunday Ticket, in-market via CBS or Fox on YouTube TV, in-market via Paramount+ or Fox One on YouTube

Sunday Night Football: NBC via YouTube TV, Peacock via YouTube

Monday Night Football: ABC/ESPN via YouTube TV, not available on YouTube

NFL Sunday Ticket also does not include preseason or postseason games, as well as some regular season games such as Thanksgiving Day games.

For Week 1 games being played on September 13, YouTube details what games will be broadcast via CBS and Fox and, as such, are not on Sunday Ticket if you live within the local region. So, as an example: If you live in Buffalo, NY, CBS will be broadcasting the Bills at Texans game, which will not be available via Sunday Ticket, but that game will be on Sunday Ticket if you live in Washington, DC.

title: Xbox Game Pass will get a Google TV app ‘in the coming months,’ likely only for TCL
snippet: Following a prior teaser that was the better part of a year ago, Microsoft has finally acknowledged its work on a Google TV app for Xbox Game Pass on TCL TVs, but it’s still “months” out from the sound of it. more…
fullText:
Following a prior teaser that was the better part of a year ago, Microsoft has finally acknowledged its work on a Google TV app for Xbox Game Pass on TCL TVs, but it’s still “months” out from the sound of it.

TCL first announced that an Xbox Game Pass app would be coming to its TVs – the Google TV models, specifically – back at CES 2026. That was in January. Microsoft never acknowledged the announcement publicly, and it’s been months since we’ve gotten any updates.

Today, Microsoft has officially confirmed that it will release an Xbox Game Pass app on TCL TVs, marking the first time the cloud gaming service will officially be available on Google TV. Microsoft’s announcement never formally acknowledges Google TV by name, hinting that this is probably exclusive to TCL TVs, rather than being available for the broader platform. TCL is the biggest Google TV partner and, while it also produces Roku and Fire TV units, it primarily uses Google TV and had previously teased the Xbox app directly around its new Google TV flagship.

But the Xbox Game Pass app for TCL’s Google TV sets is apparently still “months” away, despite the nine-month gap we’ve already gone through since the collaboration was first announced.

	

Microsoft says:

Today, we’re sharing a new partnership with TCL that will bring the XBOX app to select TCL Smart TVs in the coming months…

…With the XBOX app on supported TCL Smart TVs, players will be able to access XBOX Cloud Gaming through their Game Pass subscription to stream supported games directly from their TV. For eligible XBOX Game Pass subscribers, that means access to an instant library of games spanning blockbuster releases, beloved franchises, and indie favorites through their cloud playtime.

This comes just a day after Microsoft announced major changes to its cloud gaming setup on Xbox Game Pass. Players will now have a limited number of hours per month, topping out at 15 hours, before they need to pay more. 

Xbox Cloud Gaming will limit players to 15 hours per month before they have to pay more

title: Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra: The Highest-End Phones Compared
snippet: The iPhone 18 Pro Max has a big camera upgrade – and a bigger price. How does it compare to Samsung’s flagship phone?
fullText:
Apple’s $1,299 iPhone 18 Pro Max now stands tall as the company’s newest nonfolding high-end flagship phone. Announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday, it packs big camera and battery upgrades. But with a starting price that’s $100 higher than the iPhone 17 Pro Max, the phone’s 256GB model is now priced closely to Samsung’s $1,300 Galaxy S26 Ultra.

While every iPhone received a $100 price increase that’s likely influenced by the ongoing RAM shortage, Apple’s topline iPhone appears to be a close rival to the S26 Ultra in several key areas, especially when it comes to battery life and cameras.

The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra.

Andrew Lanxon/CNET

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra design and display

While Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro Max and Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra are big phones, their design aesthetics are quite different. The 18 Pro Max sports a similar aluminum unibody design to the one that debuted on last year’s 17 Pro Max. It comes in burgundy red, glacier blue, silver and black colors. Its shape gives it a hefty appearance, but one that fits in well when the phone is being used as a professional camera for events like Apple TV’s Major League Baseball broadcasts. And at 249 grams (8.8 ounces), the 18 Pro Max isn’t lightweight by any stretch. The phone has a 6.8-inch OLED display that should be quite expansive for videos, websites and games.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra has a slightly bigger 6.9-inch AMOLED display, but at 214 grams, it’s notably lighter than the iPhone 18 Pro Max. It also comes in six colors: pink gold, silver shadow, cobalt violet, sky blue, white and black. The S26 Ultra is also the thinnest in its line, but its Privacy Display is its most unique feature. The S26 Ultra’s display can make specific apps or notifications difficult to see from off-angle viewing, making it easier to hide content from prying eyes without needing to apply a privacy screen protector. No other company has replicated Samsung’s Privacy Display, which does make the phone stand out.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max in glacier blue.Apple/CNET

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra battery capacity

Both phones have big batteries. While Apple doesn’t disclose its battery specs in the US — instead citing that it can play 45 hours of video — its Ireland website claims the physical SIM edition will have a 5,391-mAh capacity. That’s slightly higher than the 5,000-mAh capacity on the S26 Ultra and might be even higher on the eSIM model that will be sold in the US.

Apple hasn’t yet disclosed the charging speed for the iPhone 18 Pro Max, but this is an area where Samsung already excels — the S26 Ultra has 60-watt wired charging and won our CNET Lab Test award for fastest wired charging phone by recharging from 0% to 76% in 30 minutes. That said, last year’s iPhone 17 Pro Max had a 40-watt charging speed that was one of our top performers, recharging 0% to 69% in the same 30-minute test. We look forward to testing out the 18 Pro Max to see how it fares.

You can turn on Privacy Display in Quick Settings to prevent others from seeing what’s on your screen.

Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Both phones also have their respective companies’ highest-end cameras, with Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro Max now featuring a variable-aperture camera that can physically open or close to take better photos in darker or lighter environments. This feature comes with the Pro Max’s three-camera setup that includes a 49-megapixel wide camera, a 48-megapixel ultrawide camera and a 48-megapixel telephoto camera with a 4x optical zoom. While the S26 Ultra doesn’t include a variable aperture, it has four cameras on the back that include a 200-megapixel main camera, a 50-megapixel ultrawide, a 50-megapixel telephoto with a 5x optical zoom and a 10-megapixel telephoto with a 3x optical zoom. 

	

			

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra processor, features

Apple’s A20 Pro processor powers the company’s latest AI features, headlined by the new Siri AI assistant that is built with Apple’s collaboration with Google’s Gemini. It can help you look up specific information buried in your emails and texts and turn them into actionable items like new reminders or calendar events. Apple also made a point of showing off the A20 Pro’s gaming abilities and how the phone’s vapor chamber helps keep it running cool while pushing intensive graphics. 

But Samsung’s phone includes Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 for Galaxy processor, powering its own slate of Galaxy AI features focused on proactive suggestions, along with photo editing. It’s also quite capable of high-end gaming.

fullText:
Following today’s announcement of the iPhone Duo, Apple has launched a new set of resources to help developers prepare their apps for the company’s first foldable iPhone. Here are the details.

fullText:
Today following its “Surprise and shine” September event, Apple has shipped the RC (release candidate) versions of iPadOS 27, watchOS 27, and more.

RC versions of iPadOS 27 and more available now for testing

Apple’s major new software updates for iPhone, iPad, Mac, and more are almost here.

iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS Golden Gate, watchOS 27, tvOS 27, and visionOS 27 will ship to all users next week on Monday, September 14.

After a full summer of beta testing, today Apple is rolling out the RC versions of those updates.

Developers and public beta testers can install the RC for iPadOS 27 and more via the Software Update screen in Settings.

Release candidate builds are intended to be the final shipping software that launches to all users. But if Apple discovers any critical issues that need to be patched, we may see RC 2 builds debut soon.

It’s become common practice for Apple to ship the RC builds of its major new software updates right after the annual iPhone launch event. 

That’s because there are often new features not announced at WWDC that remain hidden until the September event. For example, today Apple detailed watchOS 27 changes during the Apple Watch hardware unveiling that were not mentioned in June—but are now available in the watchOS 27 RC.

Here are the new features:

Redesigned internals

Next-generation Adaptive EQ

title: Schools are catching on to Big Tech’s playbook
snippet: It's the hot new thing in tech, and it's where all the jobs are. Students who don't learn to use it fall behind. And to help them catch up in time, its creators are graciously providing the resources and curriculum for learning it, often pro bono. That's the narrative AI companies are pitching schools on right now, but according to New York Times education technology reporter Natasha Singer, it's also how the tech industry has built its influence in classrooms for the past 15 years. In a new book, Coding Kids, Singer details how tech companies took a central role in promoting computers and coding skills in education, promising computer sci … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
It’s the hot new thing in tech, and it’s where all the jobs are. Students who don’t learn to use it fall behind. And to help them catch up in time, its creators are graciously providing the resources and curriculum for learning it, often pro bono.

That’s the narrative AI companies are pitching schools on right now, but according to New York Times education technology reporter Natasha Singer, it’s also how the tech industry has built its influence in classrooms for the past 15 years.

In a new book, Coding Kids, Singer details how tech companies took a central role in promoting computers and coding skills in education, promising computer science skills were the ticket to high-paying jobs. But by the time many of those students entered the workforce, new technologies had thrown that promise into question. Meanwhile, the companies got schools to help them create a new class of would-be workers, and trained students on using their products and software, making them likely future customers.

“I worry we have collective amnesia”

Now, the AI industry is pitching itself to schools with similar force. “I worry we have collective amnesia,” Singer told me on a recent episode of The Vergecast. “Have we learned any lessons from these past tech cycles in schools that are going to inform the rollout of AI, make sure that it benefits education, and put in the safeguards now — not a decade from now?” Fortunately, in some ways, she believes the answer is yes.

Singer’s book recounts how more than a decade ago, the country’s largest tech companies embedded themselves directly into school curricula through courses for Advanced Placement Computer Science Principles classes. Apple and Microsoft each created their own curricula, featuring their own tools like Apple’s Swift or Microsoft’s Minecraft. “What’s striking about this is you can imagine that parents would not want, say, Pfizer AP Biology, or Northrop Grumman AP Physics, or ExxonMobil Environmental Science AP,” Singer says. She found that those in the medical field would likely understand why — medical students who are trained by a company on how to implant their proprietary device, one expert told her as an example, rarely choose to try another.

Google has also made itself a dominant force in education through its distribution of low-cost laptops called Chromebooks. Singer tracked their ubiquitous adoption across schools through the 2010s, which she says was accelerated even further during the school shutdowns of the covid-19 pandemic. Google also introduced its Classroom app to help teachers communicate things like assignments and grades. By the time generative AI took off, Singer writes, Google was already a key platform provider for many schools, and well-positioned to promote it.

Even when companies weren’t directly involved in education, they backed nonprofit groups like Code.org. Code.org kicked off its viral education campaign with a splashy celebrity-laden video that included tech moguls like Microsoft founder Bill Gates and then-Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg, urging kids to learn to code. Code.org founder Hadi Partovi took a startup-style approach to promoting computer science education, and had little planned for how to capitalize on the attention of the video once it took off, Singer writes. He ultimately funneled that attention into a similarly splashy “Hour of Code” campaign across the country, urging schools to engage in entertaining hour-long courses introducing kids to coding building blocks.

At the time, there wasn’t much pushback, Singer found — though there were some attempts at alternatives. One group of academics engaged in a more traditional, methodological approach to testing and rolling out their own computer science curriculum. It had the express goal of diversifying the kinds of students enrolled in such courses, and taught students to think about big questions around the internet and technology, and scrutinize builders’ motivations.

Eventually, backlash arrived. Some recent graduates say they feel let down that they were told to code their whole lives, just to find such entry-level jobs to be diminishing, Singer told me. Some schools are getting rid of ubiquitous Google Chromebooks, and research around the world is finding that adding technology to the classroom often doesn’t have a significant impact on actual learning.

“Most parents want more than just getting kids to learn to use tech”

“I’m not arguing against tech education or tech in schools,” Singer says. “But what I am saying is most parents want more than just getting kids to learn to use tech. They want kids to learn how to be informed citizens in a democracy, and they want kids to figure out what their passions are and who they are and what their beliefs are… And so if we let the tech industry dictate or even heavily influence what happens in schools, then the question we’re asking is, how can we get AI into schools faster? Which is a product question, and not, ‘What are the most important things we want kids to learn?’”

While the AI industry of the 2020s may be pulling from the 2010s playbook, there already appears to be one distinct difference: Parents and school districts are pushing back. Just last week, the nation’s largest school system, New York City, banned elementary and middle schools from letting students use AI in the classroom for the coming school year. A day later, Los Angeles announced an even broader restriction that included high schoolers. And unlike the few-and-far-between critiques Singer documented in the early days of tech’s coding push, there appears to be a vibrant grassroots movement fighting the screen- and AI-ification of the classroom among parents and teachers alike.

“I think schools are beginning to figure it out,” says Singer, who’s “optimistic” that teachers and students are looking for a broader kind of tech education. That curriculum could teach kids “to ask deep questions about how companies are steering us with their technology, how software and AI are designed to affect our choices, and what role students have to use the tools productively. But also to push back if they like, and to not feel like they’re in a world where AI is driving them.”

Lauren Feiner

title: Google’s hyper-personalized ‘Dreambeans’ feed is now free to test [U]
snippet: Dreambeans is an experimental app from Google Labs that will “proactively dream up personalized daily stories.” After previously requiring a subscription, Dreambeans is now available for free Google Accounts in the US to test. more…
fullText:
Dreambeans is an experimental app from Google Labs that will “proactively dream up personalized daily stories.” After previously requiring a subscription, Dreambeans is now available for free Google Accounts in the US to test.

Update 9/10: Google officially announced the broader availability today.

Personalized topics: This could be everything from places to explore, shows to watch, or a reminder of upcoming events.

Connected apps: Distilled information from the Google apps you select, including Calendar, Gmail, Photos, Search, YouTube, and now Gemini.

Original 8/28: Dreambeans is very much like a hyper-personalized Google Now or Discover feed. Like the Gemini app and AI Mode, it uses Google’s Personal Intelligence system to learn your interests by looking at your Gmail, Google Photos, Calendar, Workspace, Search history, and YouTube. During setup, you can choose which apps Dreambeans can access.

Workspace supplies ground-truth transaction data like receipts and upcoming flights

Photos provides the visual memories and insights about you and the people in your life

YouTube identifies your active hobbies

Search detects your budding interests

By combining all these unique signals, Dreambeans can proactively generate rich and highly customized daily visual stories.

The app suggests topics to explore, things to try, places to visit, and interesting events. New stories arrive every morning.

	

Instead of using stock imagery, each Dreambeans story is accompanied by Nano Banana 2-generated artwork that uses an illustrated style. For example, if Dreambeans recommends a hike, you might see yourself and a group of friends at that location.

Tapping on a story lets you see a longer description. In the same example, you’ll get trail details, specific places to stop, what to wear, and timing recommendations. Dreambeans will link to trail guide content on the web. There’s also an “Ask anything” chat experience to get more information.

You can leave feedback by tapping the heart or downvoting, while the chat interface allows you to provide more details. “Tune your feed” lets you tell Dreambeans what you “want more stories about” and what it should never show.

The name combines two ideas at the heart of the app. The “dream” is how the app works overnight to find meaning in the content overload across your connected apps. It then distills what it finds into “beans” – a fresh collection of stories brewed for you each morning.

In June, it was just available for Google AI Ultra subscribers, with Google expanding to AI Pro earlier this month. The setup process “requires up to a day to build your first set of stories.” 

It remains to be seen how Dreambeans will graduate from Google Labs. The experience it offers today is largely standalone, with Daily Brief in the Gemini app possibly benefiting from a more visual experience. 

Dreambeans is available on Android and iOS in the US.

title: iPhone Duo is no Apple Vision Pro
snippet: Look, no offense to Apple Vision Pro. I’m sure Apple Vision Pro is a very nice person. But iPhone Duo and Apple Vision Pro are not the same. There’s a take that the iPhone Duo may have the Apple Vision Pro problem. The idea is that due to its price and device-specific software, it may be a miss and not a hit. The two things are not the same. more…
fullText:
Look, no offense to Apple Vision Pro. I’m sure Apple Vision Pro is a very nice person. But iPhone Duo and Apple Vision Pro are not the same.

There’s a take that the iPhone Duo may have the Apple Vision Pro problem. The idea is that due to its price and device-specific software, it may be a miss and not a hit.  The two things are not the same.

iPhone Duo doesn’t suffer from Apple Vision Pro’s biggest challenges

The biggest problem with this view is that Apple Vision Pro doesn’t replace core devices. It can be a portable movie theater and a better viewport into gaming, and mixed reality experiences can be really moving.

Apple Vision Pro doesn’t replace your iPhone or your iPad. It’s an immersive world that can fit in a suitcase. Apple Vision Pro is mostly a stationary appliance. It’s not a small tablet that can fit in your pocket that you’ll use literally everywhere you go.

Then there’s price. iPhone Duo’s $1999 starting price is a lot, but it’s not as bad as we’d feared. People are willing to pay for premium smartphones. That’s just a result of how important phones are to modern life. 

Apple Vision Pro’s original $3,499 starting price was never very palatable. Now it starts at $3,699. You can almost buy two iPhone Duos. That’s iPhone Quattro money. 

Utility, portability, and affordability all feed into the biggest difference. Apple Vision Pro fails as a mainstream consumer product for all of these reasons. As a result, it struggles to fully realize its potential.

iPhone Duo is both an iPhone and a small iPad

iPhone Duo has the utility of an iPhone and a small iPad in a form factor that can fit in your pocket. It’s also the same price as say, buying an iPhone 16 Pro one year and upgrading to the iPhone 17 Pro the next year. That’s not unheard of.

Sure, iPhone Duo will have an uphill battle with software optimization, at least for third-party apps. But Apple has already crafted a highly considered story around the operating system and first-party apps. Developers will soon have the tools to make great apps for the versatile folding display as well.

The biggest challenge with the iPhone Duo, to me, is that it’s not the absolute best-in-class iPhone yet. Hopefully it can be in some future version.

	

It would be great to have the best of every iPhone in one device, including the foldable display. But for now, the iPhone 18 Pro still wins in the camera department and Face ID.

Importantly, those trade-offs won’t be missed for consumers curious to try a radically new iPhone form factor. 

In the kindest way possible, Apple Vision Pro wishes it had iPhone Duo’s challenges.

title: What an Ex-Anthropic Researcher’s Warning About Human Extinction Really Means
snippet: AI companies think their creations could kill us all. They’re carrying on anyway.
fullText:
A string of posts on X from an AI researcher who says he quit a job at Anthropic over ethical concerns has gone viral, prompting thousands of responses and reigniting debate over the potential future dangers of artificial intelligence.

Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher who also worked at OpenAI on pretraining AI models, resigned from Anthropic over concerns that AI development could lead to human extinction. “Neither company is acting responsibly,” he wrote. “They are racing to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Superintelligence refers to a hypothetical scenario in which AI’s “cognitive” abilities vastly exceed those of humans across every domain — science, math, strategy, creativity and problem-solving. 

The threaded post on X from Coxon has more than 156 million views as of this writing and has been liked more than 752,000 times.

I resigned from Anthropic today. I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives. More thoughts below.

— Jacob Coxon (@hilbertspaess) September 9, 2026

The statement quickly spread on social media and was featured on major news sites. It even drew a comment from Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who responded on X, “It’s becoming more clear the threat AI poses to humanity, so I’m calling for immediate action from the industry and Washington.”

In less than 24 hours, the statement also drew responses from others at Anthropic who, rather than debating with Coxon, confirmed that the threat that AI will overtake and potentially eliminate humans is not a wild fantasy but a reality for AI researchers.

“Jacob [Coxon] is correct here,” wrote Evan Hubinger, a team leader at Anthropic in AI alignment stress testing, on X. Hubinger wrote in his response, “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.”

Hubinger said, “I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.”

Representatives for Anthropic and OpenAI didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Resignations that act as warning signs

It’s difficult to dismiss Coxon’s concerns for one big reason: He’s not the first researcher at a major AI company to leave for these reasons. In February, a safety lead at Anthropic, Mrinank Sharma, resigned from the company, telling followers on X, “The world is in peril … We appear to be approaching a threshold where our wisdom must grow in equal measure to our capacity to affect the world, lest we face the consequences.”

In the same month, OpenAI researcher Zoë Hitzig wrote in a New York Times column that she quit the company in part because it was following Meta’s path of putting profits ahead of ethics. Days later, she reposted a poem she’d written on X, titled “How We Programmed the Apocalypse.”

Since then, AI leaders such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have walked back some of their previous comments about AI’s potential for harm or whether it will create mass unemployment. Anthropic publicly acknowledged earlier this year that it has loosened some of its safety standards to keep up with competitors, including OpenAI and a swath of Chinese companies that have been releasing cheaper, high-performing AI models.

That competition, with both OpenAI and Anthropic hurtling toward initial public offerings, has raised concerns that, instead of moving cautiously in deploying AI models, industry leaders are rushing into the unknown and releasing models that could pose present and future dangers. This was the case when Anthropic released advanced AI models, which ended up being pulled or temporarily restricted due to major cybersecurity risks.

In the case of Coxon, whose resignation has caused the largest stir yet among those who’ve left AI companies, the dangers of contributing to the technology’s accelerating pace outweighed any financial gains. “I left before any of my equity vested,” he told the news site Axios.

Ironically, both OpenAI and Anthropic have taken the stance that if they slow down, someone less concerned with safety will drive AI’s future.

“Coxon is right that competition is driving the speed,” said Shama Hyder, a professor of AI at Link School of Business. “Every one of these companies believes slowing down hands the lead to someone less careful, so even the people who understand the risk have a reason to accelerate. “

AGI and superhuman AI 

How quickly AI poses an imminent threat to humanity may depend on when the technology reaches two purported benchmarks that have become increasingly blurred: superhuman AI (also known as artificial superintelligence or ASI), which Coxon mentioned in his viral post, and AGI, or artificial general intelligence.

AGI would mark the hypothetical point at which AI meets (or exceeds) the capabilities of a human mind. Some predict that AI will achieve that benchmark in just a few years, or at least sometime before the end of the 21st century. That timeline has also been thrown into doubt by some AI leaders, such as Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, who downplayed the importance of such markers on a recent earnings call where he said, “For many tasks, we could say that we have already achieved AGI.” The milestones, he said, “are kind of senseless at this point.”

The goalposts are also varied. Some may choose to measure AGI using specific tests, while others would consider AGI achieved only if AI could act autonomously in ways that surpass human capabilities.

ASI would be further down the road, after AGI, and would theoretically mark the point at which AI could outperform all humans across all tasks, particularly in deep thinking and cognitive understanding. The timeline for that is much fuzzier, but the speed at which AI is advancing has researchers such as Coxon suggesting it’s sooner than many people think.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman (left) and US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick (right) on stage at the G20 forum this month. Altman has acknowledged the risks of AI while trying to sway the public on the technology’s benefits.Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

A recent event that may have some adjusting their timeframes is the incident exposed in July in which OpenAI agents went rogue, plotted together and hacked Hugging Face, an AI community that was acquired by Nvidia. The speed at which the Hugging Face incident played out and the likelihood that it could happen again — this time without warning — have fueled warnings about the dangers of autonomous AI systems.

Doomers vs. boosters

The debate over whether or not AI will kill all humans by 2030 mirrors the broader discussion over AI doomers versus boosters, and the lack of nuance in the middle. While AI boosters typically hype AI by emphasizing its extraordinary potential, such as huge productivity gains, AI doomers hype it in the opposite direction, emphasizing job loss and human extinction. 

As Emily Bender and Alex Hanna argue in their book The AI Con, both AI boosters and doomers rely on science-fiction tropes to frame superintelligence as either a utopian savior or an apocalyptic threat, despite a lack of evidence that such technology is near. Many AI critics argue that either narrative functions as corporate marketing, with the same underlying premise, falsely presenting an all-powerful AI future as an absolute inevitability.

The speed at which Coxon’s post went viral and the response it’s drawing may be an indication that the AI industry has another PR crisis on its hands in a year when AI data centers are under fire and trying to change their image, and social media companies, including Meta, are reeling from multibillion-dollar judgments over issues like tech addiction.

One approach that AI leaders like Altman have taken is to focus the public’s attention on what AI brings to the table and what it could offer beyond job losses and mass death  — in other words, swapping doomer rhetoric for booster rhetoric.

“Abundance” has been a buzzword that’s been thrown around of late, promising a world in which AI’s advances and benefits will eliminate scarcity and improve life for everybody by lowering barriers to creating new goods and services and providing them more cheaply, and not just for those who can afford the costs of advanced AI technology.

Hyder said that what was missing from Coxon’s post was guidance on what people outside the AI industry can do. “The extinction debate belongs to a few hundred people who control training runs and the regulators who can inspect them,” she said. 

The question ultimately boils down to what humans want to do with the technology. “If AI is powerful enough to do the dramatic things people fear, it’s powerful enough to do the dramatic things we’ve been hoping for in medicine and science,” Hyder said.

So far, the hyped-up abundance argument has been met with skepticism, especially when it keeps public attention and fascination focused on AI. Boosterism benefits the companies that are guzzling investment dollars and promoting the billions (or trillions) their companies’ IPOs may represent.

Who cares about abundance, you could argue, if there are no humans left in the world to enjoy it? 

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Omar Gallaga
						

						

											

								

											Omar Gallaga has covered technology, digital culture and other topics for outlets including CNET, NPR, WIRED, Texas Monthly, MSNBC, Consumer Reports, The Washington Post, the Los Angeles Times, The Atlantic and the Austin American-Statesman, where he was a longtime tech reporter, editor and podcaster. He lives in the Texas Hill Country.
