title: iPhone Duo is thicker and heavier than basically every Android foldable
snippet: The days of foldables being an Android-only experience are over. The iPhone Duo is set to arrive next month for a relatively-competitive $2,000 price point, and it seems like Apple’s decision to sit back and observe since the launch of the original Galaxy Fold more or less paid off — that is, until you consider the iPhone Duo’s size and shape. more…
fullText:
The days of foldables being an Android-only experience are over. The iPhone Duo is set to arrive next month for a relatively-competitive $2,000 price point, and it seems like Apple’s decision to sit back and observe since the launch of the original Galaxy Fold more or less paid off — that is, until you consider the iPhone Duo’s size and shape.

I won’t lie — there’s plenty of things I find intriguing about the iPhone Duo. Sure, it apes almost everything we know about modern folding phones from Samsung and Google, but with a couple of interesting twists. Keeping the under-display camera and stylus support from earlier Galaxy Z-series entries? A very smooth transition between inner and outer displays? A Made You Look clone but with Snoopy? I might prefer Android to iOS, but at the end of the day, I’m only human.

But no matter how “modern” the iPhone Duo appears at first glance compared to Google and Samsung’s respective first-gen entries, it loses out on one big metric: bulk. The iPhone Duo measures in at 11.3mm thick when closed and weighs a whopping 254 grams. Compared to Apple’s most recent foldable rivals, that’s 15 grams (or three nickels worth) heavier than the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, 39 grams heavier than the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, and a whopping 53 grams heavier than the similarly-shaped Fold 8. Each of those phones is significantly thinner too, ranging anywhere between 8.9mm to 10.1mm when closed.

iPhone Duo: 254g, 11.3mm closed

Pixel 11 Pro Fold: 239g, 10.1mm closed

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra: 215g, 8.9mm closed

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: 201g, 9.7mm closed

It is, undoubtedly, a miss from Apple’s design, especially considering the push for lightweight devices with last year’s iPhone Air. However — and here’s where I have betray the most dedicated Android fans just a tiny bit — while I absolutely think Apple’s foldable is bulkier and heavier than it should be in 2026, I can’t pretend like Google is that far ahead here. Yes, this year’s foldable finally managed to shed a few grams, but the iPhone Duo still manages to be lighter than 2025’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold, a device Google was pushing to users but a month ago. Samsung, though? It’s eating Apple’s lunch all day.

	

I also have no idea how much of that extra bulk can be chalked up to Apple Pencil support. Samsung upset a pretty sizable portion of its audience when it dropped the S Pen from the Galaxy Z Fold 7, but that sacrifice came with a significantly slimmer and lighter chassis. Comparing the iPhone Duo to 2024’s Fold 6 — the last foldable Samsung shipped with stylus support — it measures in at 12.1mm thick. That said, the Fold 6 still had Apple beat on weight, even with a device that’s now over two years old.

At the end of the day, the size and weight of the iPhone Duo really only matters if you’re completely platform-agnostic, a foldable-first fan who simply wants the most refined hardware experience around. I expect most Android fans won’t be tempted with a big-screen experience not all too dissimilar from what they’ve had access to for the better part of a decade now, and I expect iOS fans who have held out for an Apple-made foldable won’t be put off by a device that’s a bit bulkier than its rivals. But hey, if you’re an early adopter looking to lord something over your Apple-loving co-workers in a couple of months, you’ve already found your first opportunity.

title: Pixel 11 gets early September update, not Android 17 QPR1 [U: OTA images]
snippet: We’re expecting the stable release of Android 17 QPR1 in September. Before that, Google is rolling out an out-of-cycle update to the Pixel 11 series with a September 2026 security patch. more…
fullText:
We’re expecting the stable release of Android 17 QPR1 in September. Before that, Google is rolling out an out-of-cycle update to the Pixel 11 series with a September 2026 security patch.

Update 9/9: Following the on-device update that some users received last week, Google has posted updated factory and OTA images for manual install. The September 1 patch ended in A1, while today’s release is B1.

It comes as not all users received last week’s OTA, with Google appearing to pull the update at some point. Those that received the previous update are getting another one that comes in at 97~ MB.  

The four updates for the Pixel 11, 11 Pro, 11 Pro XL, and 11 Pro Fold are labeled “Sep 2026.” Curiously, Google has yet to announce the Android 17 QPR1 update and expected Pixel Drop.

	

Original 9/1: On Tuesday afternoon, Pixel 11 series users received an OTA update to CD1A.260905.001.A1 (from CD1A.260714.001.A9).

The Android security update level is “September 1, 2026.” (Note: Not September 5.) The install screen has the usual generic security message: “This update fixes critical bugs and improves the performance and stability of your device.”

So far, we have reports of an under 100 MB OTA hitting the Pixel 11 Pro, 11 Pro XL, and 11 Pro Fold. Google has yet to post factory or OTA images as of Tuesday afternoon.

This is not Android 17 QPR1. Several of the visual changes coming in that release are not yet present, so this is still the initial release of Android 17.

Rather, Google is likely rolling out this update as a hot patch for Pixel 11 issues discovered since last month’s launch. The fact Google did not wait for Android 17 QPR1 should be telling.

title: New Apple TV 4K will be more powerful upgrade than we thought, per leak
snippet: Rumors about the new Apple TV 4K have long suggested it will have a more modern chip to enable Apple Intelligence support. But a new leak uncovered by Aaron Perris points to an even more powerful chip than previously expected. more…
fullText:
Rumors about the new Apple TV 4K have long suggested it will have a more modern chip to enable Apple Intelligence support. But a new leak uncovered by Aaron Perris points to an even more powerful chip than previously expected.

Apple TV 4K coming soon will have A19 or A19 Pro chip, per code leak

We’ve been waiting a long time for a new Apple TV 4K. Longer than any other moment in the product’s history.

We discovered a reference to Apple’s upcoming Apple TV model, AppleTV18,1

Implications being it will have A19 or A19 Pro

	

The ‘18,1’ numbering scheme echoes the identifiers used by Apple’s iPhone 17 line last year. Some iPhone 17 models had an A19 chip, while iPhone Air and the 17 Pro line used A19 Pro.

Either chip would be a sizable upgrade for the Apple TV. But I wonder if the A19 Pro is more likely to be used because it exclusively supports Siri AI’s most advanced features.

Siri AI is expected to be one of the tentpole additions to the new Apple TV 4K. Considering how long it’s been between hardware updates, I hope Apple doesn’t immediately launch a new model that misses out on some AI capabilities.

title: iPhone Ultra is coming, here’s what the final rumors say
snippet: Apple is expected to announce its first-ever foldable iPhone tomorrow, which rumors say could be called the iPhone Ultra. Here are some last-minute rumors about what to expect. more…
fullText:
Apple is expected to announce its first-ever foldable iPhone tomorrow, which rumors say could be called the iPhone Ultra. Here are some last-minute rumors about what to expect.

Starting price

In a new report today, Bloomberg said Apple was initially targeting a $1,999 starting price for the iPhone Ultra. However, due to rising component costs, Apple has most recently discussed a $2,199 starting price. iPhone Ultra configurations with more storage could stretch to $3,000, according to the report.

Delayed launch in China

In a post on Weibo today, leaker Instant Digital said the foldable iPhone will likely launch later in China than the rest of the world. This is primarily due to the device being eSIM-only, and eSIM adoption and infrastructure in China lag behind that of other countries.

The iPhone Air also launched later in China than elsewhere due to regulatory issues surrounding its eSIM-only design.

More evidence of Touch ID

In a post on social media this week, developer Pdfu shared more evidence that the iPhone Ultra will use Touch ID instead of Face ID. This, of course, has been widely reported as one of the device’s limitations, so this is just another layer of corroboration.

iPhone Ultra display crease

Apple set out to make a foldable iPhone without a visible crease, unlike other foldable phones on the market. In a report today, Bloomberg said the company has ultimately created a “crease that is far less visible than on currently shipping foldables.” To accomplish this, Apple developed an “advanced titanium-and-aluminum hinge system paired with custom cover glass.”

So even though it’s not completely creaseless, this is still something Apple “plans to highlight as a major competitive advantage.”

MagSafe

One conflicting rumor has been whether the iPhone Ultra will feature support for MagSafe. Mark Gurman had good news on this front in a recent interview. “MagSafe is there. All indications that I’ve heard are that MagSafe is in for this foldable phone,” he said.

Wrap up

title: iPhone Duo vs. Pixel 11 Pro Fold: 2 Durable Foldables Face Off
snippet: Apple’s and Google’s phones are both rated for dust and water resistance. Here’s how they compare when it comes to other features such as cameras, battery life and displays.
fullText:
Companies often focus on features like thinness and screen size when launching foldable phones. But for many people, one of the biggest concerns is durability. If you’re spending around $2,000 on a phone, you want to know it can withstand whatever life throws at it.

Apple’s iPhone Duo and Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold stand out in the increasingly competitive foldable phone market for one notable reason: They both have IP68 ratings. That means they’re expected to withstand being submerged in water (up to 6 meters for the Duo and 1.5 meters for the Pixel) for up to 30 minutes, and are dust resistant — a rarity in the world of foldables. So in theory, you can take your pricey handset to the beach without worrying about sand getting in and ruining your device.

The two phones also have high price tags. The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 for 256GB, while the Pixel 11 Pro Fold starts at $1,899 for the same storage level. Preorders for the iPhone Duo kick off Oct. 16, for an Oct. 23 release. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is available now.

	

			

I’ve had the opportunity to use both phones, and the key difference lies in how each is designed. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold takes on a more traditional book-style design, with a cover screen resembling the measurements of a standard slab phone. Inside, the expansive screen is ideal for watching movies or multitasking.

On the other hand, the Duo’s passport-size design makes for a squatter, more compact cover screen and a short, wide inner display that’s ideal for watching videos in landscape and is well-suited to vertical content in portrait. Like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, it’s designed to adapt more naturally to a wider range of content formats.

Here’s how else the iPhone Duo and Pixel 11 Pro Fold compare. 

iPhone Duo vs. Pixel 11 Pro Fold design and displays

The iPhone Duo has a 5.4-inch cover display.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

The iPhone Duo has a squat, 5.4-inch cover display and a wide, 7.6-inch inside display. Meanwhile, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a taller 6.5-inch cover display and a larger 8-inch main display.

The Duo can be a good fit if you want something compact that essentially expands into an iPad Mini. The Pixel Fold feels very much like a non-folding phone when closed, and opens up to a more expansive, tablet-like display.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a 6.5-inch cover screen made with a new glass ceramic that’s more resistant to scratches and cracks, according to Google.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

A key differentiator is the iPhone Duo has a matte, nano-texture inner display that helps to reduce reflections and minimize the crease. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold doesn’t have an anti-reflective display, which makes the phone’s crease more visible. 

Both phones are relatively thin. The iPhone Duo measures 5.2mm thick when open and 11.3mm thick when closed. It weighs 254 grams.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has the iPhone slightly beat, measuring 5mm thick when open and 10.1mm thick when closed. It’s also a little lighter than the iPhone, weighing 239 grams. That’s likely aided by the Pixel 11 Pro Fold’s aluminum frame, compared to the titanium one on the iPhone Duo.

The iPhone Duo looks like an iPad Mini. But it isn’t. Is it?Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Both phones let you run up to two apps side by side. 

The iPhone Duo comes with a key concession: It supports only Touch ID, rather than Face ID, for unlocking. By comparison, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold supports Face Unlock.

Both the iPhone Duo and Pixel 11 Pro Fold have IP68 ratings for dust and water resistance, but the better design ultimately depends on how you plan to use the phone. If you want a device optimized for consuming a wide range of content, the versatile iPhone Duo could be a better fit. If you prefer a more traditional phone that unfolds into a larger display, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold may be the more natural choice.

The iPhone Duo has two 48-megapixel rear cameras.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

The iPhone Duo has a 48-megapixel main camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide camera. Like the similarly passport-sized Galaxy Z Fold 8, there’s no telephoto camera. A 12-megapixel selfie camera sits on the outer display, while an “under-display FaceTime camera” is nestled on the inside.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold’s shooters don’t quite live up to the camera specs on the non-folding Pro models, but they pull their weight. The foldable has a 48-megapixel wide-angle, 10.5-megapixel ultrawide and 10.8-megapixel telephoto camera on the back. There’s a 10-megapixel selfie camera on the cover and inside displays. Although the foldable Pixel doesn’t have Google’s top-of-the-line camera setup, it performed well in my camera test against another premium foldable, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a triple-rear camera system. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

When taking photos with the rear camera, both the iPhone Duo and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold allow you to preview images using the phone’s cover screen, so you can guide the photographer (or yourself if you’re taking selfies). The phones also both have features designed to draw kids’ eyes to the camera by playing animations on the cover screen, called Kid Cue on the Duo and Made You Look on the Pixel Fold.

We’ll have to see how the iPhone Duo’s cameras perform in the real world, but the Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a leg up with the inclusion of a telephoto camera.

iPhone Duo vs. Pixel 11 Pro Fold processor and battery life

Both devices pack top-end specs, though their storage options differ. The iPhone Duo runs on the new A20 Pro chip, and as usual for its phones, Apple hasn’t stated how much RAM the foldable has — but it does come in 256GB, 512GB, 1TB and 2TB options (the latter pushing the price up to a jaw-dropping $3,199 in the US).  The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a Google-designed Tensor G6 chip, 16GB of RAM and options for 256GB, 512GB and 1TB of storage.

Apple doesn’t share specific battery specs, but says the iPhone Duo will give you up to 31 hours of video playback on the inner display, and 44 hours when using the outer screen. When using both screens equally, the company says you’ll be able to go 24 hours before needing to charge.

Meanwhile, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a 4,806-mAh battery, which lasts well over a day with heavy use.

That’s not an iPad, but the iPhone Duo next to the Apple Pencil that you’ll soon be able to use with it.

Both phones support Qi2 wireless charging up to 25 watts, and have built-in magnets to easily attach accessories such as wireless chargers and wallets.

Apple says the iPhone Duo can charge up to 50% in around 20 minutes with a 60-watt adapter or higher. Wirelessly, it can charge up to 50% in around 30 minutes with a 35-watt adapter or higher when paired with a MagSafe charger.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold supports up to 30-watt wired charging, which gets the phone from 0% to 55% in 30 minutes. It takes about an hour and a half to fully charge.

Both the iPhone Duo and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold are designed to handle heavy use across their dual displays. Qi2 compatibility with built-in magnets can make wireless charging a snap. 

Which phone should you pick?

You can prop the iPhone Duo on its side to quickly glance at the time.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

The iPhone Duo and Pixel 11 Pro Fold are two foldables designed with slightly different use cases in mind. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a more conventional cover screen paired with a spacious main display. The Duo, meanwhile, has a more compact cover screen and an inner display designed to adapt to different content formats, whether you’re watching a video in landscape or viewing vertical content in portrait.

We have yet to review the iPhone Duo, but based on my limited time with the phone, I can see it appealing to anyone who wants something that feels fresh and smaller-scale. If you’re deep in the Apple ecosystem, you may have already made up your mind that this is the phone for you.

For anyone who wants to preserve the experience of using a slab phone while also tapping into a larger display, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold can be a good fit. Its thin design makes it feel so ordinary that I often mistake it for my iPhone 17 Pro Max when reaching into my bag.

We’ll know more about the Duo’s performance when we have the chance to test and review it. In the meantime, check out the chart below for more specifics about the two phones.

title: John Ternus and Greg Joswiak reveal why now is the time for iPhone Duo
snippet: Following this week’s Apple event, new Apple CEO John Ternus and marketing SVP Greg Joswiak sat down for an interview to talk more about the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. In the interview with Tom’s Guide and TechRadar, Ternus and Joswiak discussed why Apple decided that now was the time to enter the foldable market. Ternus also touched on his feelings after his first week as Apple CEO. more…
fullText:
Sc			
	

Following this week’s Apple event, new Apple CEO John Ternus and marketing SVP Greg Joswiak sat down for an interview to talk more about the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo.

In the interview with Tom’s Guide and TechRadar, Ternus and Joswiak discussed why Apple decided that now was the time to enter the foldable market. Ternus also touched on his feelings after his first week as Apple CEO.

On why Apple felt now was the time to announce iPhone Duo, Ternus explained:

“I think for us, it’s always about when do we feel like we have a product idea that meets our bar for quality and durability, but also for design. What I think is particularly amazing about the Duo is, it’s such a good example of hardware and software coming together to make something really special.

It was like a green field of opportunity for us because there was opportunity to rethink so many different things. And I think you see that in the hardware, and you see that in the software, and the design. It all kind of came together and felt like it was the right product.

Joz, meanwhile, added that what Apple saw other smartphone makers doing in the foldable space “wasn’t very inspiring.”

“If you’ve seen what’s been out there, not only is it just kind of cheap-feeling plastic surfaces, they don’t feel good to touch, they’re kind of wavy, wrinkly,” Ternus added in reference to the displays of competing foldable phones.

Ternus was also asked about the moment he first found out he was going to be CEO of Apple:

It’s amazing, what an extraordinary privilege, right? The reality is I just, I love this place. It’s in my blood. I’ve been here for half my life. I love the people I work with. I love to be able to build the products that we all build together. And so goosebumps, excitement and yeah, just real, like really, really excited about the future.

title: Someone recreated the iPhone Duo’s mesmerizing open animation on the Galaxy Z Fold 8
snippet: It’s been less than a day since Apple announced the iPhone Duo, and someone has already taken the instantly iconic Apple iPhone Duo unfolding animation and applied it to their Galaxy Z Fold 8. Don’t get too excited, because it isn’t exactly available for everyone. more…
fullText:
It’s been less than a day since Apple announced the iPhone Duo, and someone has already taken the instantly iconic Apple iPhone Duo unfolding animation and applied it to their Galaxy Z Fold 8. Don’t get too excited, because it isn’t exactly available for everyone.

If you caught any of Apple’s iPhone event, you’ll undoubtedly be familiar with the iPhone Duo. Much like Google, Apple is entering the space with a passport-sized foldable phone to appeal to a wider number of users over the taller, slimmer design Samsung pioneered for the last few years. Even Samsung has added the shorter, wider form factor to its lineup.

That’s what makes what one user did for their Galaxy Z Fold 8 such a natural next step after Apple’s announcement. Someone recreated Apple’s iPhone Duo unfolding animation for the Galaxy Z Fold 8. They shared their work on Reddit, and it looks extremely close to what the early hands-on and promo videos show on the new folding iPhone.

The animation on the iPhone Duo creates this sort of blue effect, stuck in perceived space. When you open the phone, apps and home screen content stay locked in space while it looks like your phone physically reorients itself around software. It fits right in line with the liquid glass design philosophy, with app icons coming into focus as the phone opens wider.

	

On the Galaxy Z Fold 8, it can be done by assigning hinge extension values to frames of an animation. In effect, opening the Fold 8 plays an animation at the speed the phone unfolds.

That’s where the downside of this fun little trick lies. Since it’s an animation of two screenshots with a blur effect, it can’t be built into the SystemUI. At least, not in the current state Samsung makes it available.

That doesn’t detract from the sheer hype in the comments. It’s clear that even a GoodLock copycat feature would be welcomed with open arms. If one thing was clear, the iPhone Duo shines in UX design, and competition between Android foldables and now Apple’s might mean Samsung adds more refined features that make the overall experience feel cleaner.

title: Thrive Capital led VCs into pro sports ownership; Collaborative Fund just upped that play
snippet: Collaborative Fund just bought into D.C. United and its stadium, with firm founder Craig Shapiro pitching it as a way to showcase for the firm's startups.
fullText:
Collaborative Fund, the 15-year-old, New York-based generalist venture firm that has roughly $1 billion under management and that made early bets on Lyft, Reddit, Sweetgreen, and Olipop, among others, is taking a stake in the soccer club D.C. United and its stadium, Audi Field.

It’s the latest — and smallest — firm to try something that Thrive Capital opened the door to just months ago: turning venture money into pro sports ownership.

To recap, Joshua Kushner’s Thrive launched a new vehicle, Thrive Eternal, explicitly built to hold “iconic franchises and cultural institutions” for decades, funded by many of the same investors already in Thrive’s venture and growth funds. The firm kicked things off by announcing a stake in the San Francisco Giants. Months later, the same vehicle — with former Disney CEO Bob Iger, a Thrive partner, joining as co-owner — bought the Lakers outright for a record $12.5 billion.

That’s new. Historically, money has poured into pro sports two other ways: individual tech fortunes and private equity. For example, Vinod Khosla and his family agreed this summer to buy the Seattle Seahawks for a record $9.6 billion soon after the Khosla family also took a stake in the San Francisco 49ers alongside OpenAI chairman Bret Taylor. That was a personal-wealth play, the kind we’ve seen over and over.

Private equity firms have also been at this for years, including Sixth Street, which holds stakes in the Boston Celtics, the New England Patriots, and MLB’s San Francisco Giants; Ares, which owns a piece of the Miami Dolphins outright and separately financed Chelsea’s stadium plans through a $500 million preferred-equity deal; RedBird, which owns AC Milan outright and holds a minority stake in Fenway Sports Group, the holding company behind Liverpool and the Red Sox; and Arctos, with minority positions scattered across MLB, the NFL, the NBA, and European soccer. (Apollo, the newest entrant, has mostly stuck to sports financing deals so far rather than ownership stakes.)

Thrive and Collaborative are doing neither of those things. At the same time, the two firms’ approaches to sports ownership look very different. Thrive built a stand-alone, permanent-capital vehicle specifically to hold trophy assets. Collaborative is investing out of the same early-stage fund it uses to write seed and Series A checks, and treating the deal less like something to buy and hold and almost more like infrastructure.

In a memo shared with TechCrunch, Collaborative Fund founder and managing partner Craig Shapiro framed the deal as an extension of what the firm already does. “A franchise is the ultimate consumer product,” he wrote, arguing that D.C. United’s status as one of Major League Soccer’s original clubs gives Collaborative access to an institution with a decades-long fan base to build on.

He pointed to the tailwinds around American soccer specifically (a World Cup just behind the sport, the LA Olympics ahead of it, soaring youth participation numbers in the U.S.), as well as D.C.’s ownership of Audi Field in Washington, D.C., plus a talent-development pipeline through Loudoun County, Virginia, and rights to a future Baltimore expansion team.

Indeed, the thesis Shapiro laid out at a TechCrunch StrictlyVC event Thursday night in New York is less about owning a piece of an appreciating asset — the sports team itself — and more about what the team makes possible. Collaborative wants to turn Audi Field into what he describes as a living showcase for its own portfolio.

As a backer of both fitness band maker Whoop and the beverage brand Olipop, for example, Collaborative Fund is imagining a Whoop wearables activation for fans, or Olipop drinks woven into game-day concessions. He’s thinking about the stadium’s foot traffic — tens of thousands of people showing up on a predictable schedule — as a distribution channel at a time when, because AI is making more of daily life feel synthetic, live experiences are becoming more valuable.

Shapiro doesn’t dwell on this, but it surely helped sell Collaborative’s investors that team valuations have been soaring, so the stake could pay off on its own. Soccer valuations in particular have been on a tear. Inter Miami’s franchise value has roughly doubled in the two years since Lionel Messi arrived, MLS’s average club value is up roughly 134% since 2019, and D.C. United’s own valuation has climbed from $35 million in 2008 to $785 million today, factoring in its ownership of Audi Field and the surrounding real estate.

If Shapiro is right that a franchise is also “the ultimate consumer product,” it could be a pretty good place to park money. Time will tell.

The deal is subject to MLS approval.

title: Apple made fun of Android apps on foldables, but iPhone Duo has the same problem [Gallery]
snippet: Apps have always been a problem for foldable displays and, while they’ve gotten a lot better, there’s always room for improvement. Apple was already going to hold an advantage here, as we’ve previously discussed, but a moment during the iPhone Duo’s unveiling sticks out – Apple made fun of how Android foldables sometimes letterbox apps on the inner display, but it turns out that iOS does exactly the same thing. more…
fullText:
Apps have always been a problem for foldable displays and, while they’ve gotten a lot better, there’s always room for improvement. Apple was already going to hold an advantage here, as we’ve previously discussed, but a moment during the iPhone Duo’s unveiling sticks out – Apple made fun of how Android foldables sometimes letterbox apps on the inner display, but it turns out that iOS does exactly the same thing.

In the early moments of the iPhone Duo’s announcement, new Apple CEO John Ternus called out “others” who have already launched foldables, with a background video showing the age-old problem – letterboxed apps.

To quote new Apple CEO John Ternus:

Others have created foldables that just feel like two phones awkwardly stuck together. This results in a square screen that’s poorly suited for the way people use them. Scrolling through vertical content feels compromised, and movies are boxed in by oversized black bars, making a larger screen feel much smaller.

Here’s the clip:

	

This was a pretty major problem in the early days of Android foldables. While Android apps have always been good at scaling, the unique form factors of those early days often found weird middle grounds or, even more frequently, apps just hadn’t been updated to be viewed on anything other than an ordinary smartphone display aspect ratio. At the time, it was a wise move on Google’s part, but the problem has been going away thanks to a push on Google’s part as well as the wider adoption of these form factors. Heck, Android foldables got a tablet layout for Instagram before the iPad did. 

So, while watching today’s event, my reaction to that little dig was that Apple is just finding old problems to make Android look bad, again – not exactly new behavior. 

But then our sister site 9to5Mac dug up Apple’s own documentation of how iOS 27.1 will handle apps on the foldable display and, lo and behold, Apple is doing the same thing.

If an app isn’t updated to support iOS 27, it gets boxed in with black bars on either side, showing a portrait view of the app instead. If it isn’t ready for iOS 27.1, it still can’t take up the display area off to the side where the sidebar is.

This was my actual reaction.

As mentioned, Apple has an app advantage in that iOS developers will likely be much quicker to adopt this new form factor. I’m already jealous of that Slack app Apple briefly showed; Slack, you literally had that on Android half a decade ago, bring it back.

Thoughts?

title: iPhone Duo hands-on videos reveal Android foldable pain points we know too well
snippet: Apple has a track record of waiting until the kinks get worked out before it tries its own hand at new devices, but hands-on videos of the iPhone Duo are already starting to show that Apple suffers from some of the same pain points other manufacturers like Samsung do, like the beloved screen crease. more…
fullText:
via Brian Tong			
	

Apple has a track record of waiting until the kinks get worked out before it tries its own hand at new devices, but hands-on videos of the iPhone Duo are already starting to show that Apple suffers from some of the same pain points other manufacturers like Samsung do, like the beloved screen crease.

Samsung has faced some backlash over the years as its continued to develop the Galaxy Z Fold line, as it rightfully should. Flaws exist on these $1,800+ phones, like an ever-present visible crease down the hinge line on the inner display or a less-than-invisible under-display camera.

It turns out Apple hasn’t been entirely successful at perfecting those flaws in its own design. Early hands-on videos are already starting to go live after Apple’s event in Cupertino, and more are very much on the way. Videos like this one from Brian Tong show some interesting details Apple’s keynote left out.

For one, the iPhone Duo’s inner screen is anti-reflective, but it comes off as matte more than anything. It’s a massive contrast from the outer display, which is made from Ceramic Shield 2. Sitting in stark contrast to that matte inner display is the under-display camera, which Apple showed off several times during its keynote. It’s something Samsung dropped from the Galaxy Z Fold design when it launched the latest models, for one reason or another.

	

The iPhone Duo’s under-display camera has no matte finish. That change in finish only serves to highlight a camera that’s supposed to be hidden from view.

Of course, it was never going to be completely hidden, and Apple’s pre-release footage and renders rightfully showed off a camera that was clearly hiding under an area of fewer pixels. Samsung used the same approach in the Galaxy Z Fold 6, but it’s always been just as noticeable. In reality, the camera seems far more noticeable because of the differing reflectivity.

Beyond that, we get a good look at the iPhone Duo’s inner screen crease. It was expected Apple would refine its foldable’s inner display design so a crease would be far less visible than current Android options, but the crease looks just as visible as it does on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra. Apple is using a two-layer flexible glass, which helps prevent a buildup in tension that would cause materials to bind up in the middle.

Still, the crease is a factual aspect of the iPhone Duo. That isn’t to say Apple hasn’t done a good job of hiding it, but it’s an unfortunate aspect of foldable phones for the time being.

The new foldable’s specs also reveal its IP68 water and dust resistant rating is also expected to be temporary, similar to the Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold.

If Apple excels anywhere with the iPhone Duo its in how it designed iOS 27 around the new phone. Compared to where Android and One UI are in their respective builds, Apple’s approach feels much more purposeful for a phone that forces you to look at it a different way. It’s only a matter of time before Android manufacturers begin to copy some of these UX design choices. It introduces welcome competition.

title: Hands-on with Siri Modular, watchOS 27’s new Apple Watch face
snippet: watchOS 27 includes one new watch face: Siri Modular. The new face is available on both Apple Watch Series and Ultra models. However, the version on Ultra has a few more customization options. Check it out. more…
fullText:
watchOS 27 includes one new watch face: Siri Modular. The new face is available on both Apple Watch Series and Ultra models. However, the version on Ultra has a few more customization options. Check it out.

Both versions of Siri Modular use the same layout. There’s a top center line complication, the time (centered), a wide Siri suggestion widget, and a row of three circular complications.

Apple Watch Ultra also supports bezel options, adding one more way to configure the new watch face. 

First, three style options let you adjust the height of the clock. The first option features the tallest clock and three circular complications. The second style is a compact clock with the wide Siri suggestion widget and three circular complications. The third style is a medium clock with a wide complication.

All three modes support displaying the top line complication. None of the modes support displaying the current seconds as part of the clock. 

Both Series and Ultra also include font options for the clock. However, Ultra is only an option on Apple Watch Ultra hardware. Series models only offer Modern, Classic, and Rounded.

Meanwhile, the Ultra includes those bezel options I mentioned. These are like other Ultra-exclusive watch faces.

Lastly, there’s the option to set the watch face color, including lots of new options like Dark Bronze, Radiant Gold, and other new choices.

Siri Modular is part of the new watchOS 27 update, included in today’s release candidate software.

title: iPhone Duo: Here are all the little details you might have missed
snippet: iPhone Duo is the name of Apple’s new foldable model, and it’s perhaps the most fascinating new model since the original iPhone. Here are all the little iPhone Duo details you might have missed. more…
fullText:
iPhone Duo is the name of Apple’s new foldable model, and it’s perhaps the most fascinating new model since the original iPhone. Here are all the little iPhone Duo details you might have missed.

iPhone Duo tidbits from Apple’s announcement and website

Apple’s first foldable iPhone was unveiled today ahead of becoming available to order next month.

If you’re looking to buy a new iPhone, you might be very interested in the Duo, but are unsure if it’s right for you.

Read more: iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone Duo: Here’s every key difference

The tentpole features of iPhone Duo are pretty clear: it’s a foldable, with two displays, great cameras and battery life, and plenty of unique form factor advantages.

But there were a variety of smaller iPhone Duo details revealed both in today’s announcement and on Apple’s website afterwards.

Camera features

Software exclusives: iPhone Duo has several exclusive camera features available in software, like Smart Take, Kid Cue, and Duo Preview. But most notably, its Main camera lacks the variable aperture feature of iPhone 18 Pro.

Under-display camera: A first in the iPhone, the folding display of iPhone Duo has an under-display camera for a cutout-free inner screen.

Selfie cameras are very different: That under-display camera isn’t nearly as capable as the Center Stage front camera on the outer display, so you’ll want to use the outer camera when possible.

Buttons

iPhone Duo has a Camera Control button, but is missing the Action button that’s been available on other iPhone models for several years now.

Displays

There’s a nano‑texture finish only on the folding iPhone Duo display. You won’t find nano-texture on the outer screen.

Apple Pencil

Apple says iPhone Duo will support Apple Pencil later this year on both the inner and folding displays. However, currently only the USB-C Pencil model is supported, not the Apple Pencil Pro.

Release Date

Unlike iPhone 18 Pro, which goes on sale later this week, iPhone Duo won’t be available to order until October 16. It then ships to all users a week later on October 23.

iOS 27.1

It’s probably not surprising, since iPhone Duo doesn’t ship until late October, but Apple says the new model will run iOS 27.1 when it arrives.

eSIM only

	

You won’t be able to buy an iPhone Duo with physical SIM anywhere in the world. Even in China, where users largely prefer physical SIMs, the iPhone Duo will be eSIM-only.

title: iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone Duo: Here’s every key difference
snippet: Today Apple unveiled three flagship new iPhone models: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max as well as the foldable iPhone Duo. Here’s an overview of the key differences between each model. more…
fullText:
Today Apple unveiled three flagship new iPhone models: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max as well as the foldable iPhone Duo. Here’s an overview of the key differences between each model.

Form factor and dimensions: Foldable vs traditional

It’s the most obvious difference, but should be stated regardless. With iPhone Duo you get a very different form factor: it’s a foldable device. With iPhone 18 Pro, you get a traditional iPhone experience.

If you’ve never used a foldable, it’s hard to explain the difference in how each model might feel in practice. But generally speaking, with iPhone Duo you get essentially an iPhone and iPad in one device. The displays are unique shapes and sizes compared to a traditional iPhone though, which may take some adjustment.

Here is how each model’s dimensions compare:

iPhone Duo might seem more sleek than iPhone 18 Pro Max, but it ultimately weighs slightly more.

Displays: Dual vs single in varying sizes

iPhone Duo has two displays: a 5.4-inch outer display and a 7.6-inch folding display.

With iPhone 18 Pro, you can choose from the standard 6.3-inch size or 6.9-inch Pro Max model.

So with the Duo, you can enjoy a “small iPhone” experience while also having the option of a larger inner screen than what iPhone 18 Pro Max can offer.

iPhone Duo’s folding display comes with a nano-texture finish, a first in an iPhone.

Cameras: Clear advantage for iPhone 18 Pro

Cameras are one of the most important iPhone features. And in this department, iPhone 18 Pro is the clear winner.

iPhone 18 Pro has the new 48MP Main camera with variable aperture. iPhone Duo lacks the variable aperture feature, so its Main camera lags behind the Pro line.

With iPhone 18 Pro, you also get the Telephoto camera that’s missing from iPhone Duo.

In terms of software features, each model has its own unique exclusives:

iPhone Duo: Smart Take, Kid Cue, Duo Preview

iPhone 18 Pro: Smart focus tracking, Pro controls, Apple Reference Image

iPhone 18 Pro also exclusively supports ProRes video recording up to 4K at 60 fps with external recording, a “studio-quality four-mic array,” Spatial video recording at 1080p at 30 fps, Spatial photos, ProRes RAW, Genlock, and more.

Battery: Excellent battery life on all models

Because iPhone Duo has two displays, its quoted battery life varies depending on which display you’re using. But overall, Apple is promising strong battery life on both the Duo as well as iPhone 18 Pro.

Here are Apple’s quoted numbers:

iPhone Duo outer display: Up to 44 hours

iPhone Duo folding display: Up to 31 hours

iPhone 18 Pro: Up to 36 hours

iPhone 18 Pro Max: Up to 45 hours

Everyone’s use patterns will differ, but if you split the difference between the two iPhone Duo battery estimates, you’re looking at around 38 hours in average video playback.

All the other big and small differences: Face ID, buttons, software, Apple Pencil, more

Authentication differs between iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, with the former using Touch ID and the latter Face ID.

iPhone Duo does not have an Action button, but does offer Camera Control.

iPhone Duo comes with several multitasking advantages in iOS 27, like the ability to use apps in Split View and have unique landscape views. It also has other fun software additions like a partially-folded StandBy mode.

Apple Pencil (USB-C model) will be supported on iPhone Duo later this year, another advantage over iPhone 18 Pro.

A new C2 modem is included in both iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, but curiously not iPhone 18 Pro Max.

Colors for iPhone 18 Pro are Burgundy, Glacier, Black, and Silver. iPhone Duo only offers two colors: Star White and Night Sky.

Finally, design materials differ: iPhone 18 Pro has an aluminum unibody design, while iPhone Duo uses titanium.

Pricing and availability: Big gaps in both

Pricing is another major difference between Apple’s new models. Here are starting prices for 256GB models:

iPhone Duo: $1,999

iPhone 18 Pro: $1,199

iPhone 18 Pro Max: $1,299

iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are available for pre-order this Saturday and ship next Friday, September 18. Meanwhile, iPhone Duo won’t be available for pre-order until October 16, and ships October 23.

title: iPhone 18 Pro battery life: how much better is the battery compared to iPhone Duo and iPhone 17 Pro
snippet: Apple has just announced the new flagship iPhone lineup, featuring iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. One of the biggest improvements is battery life. In fact, Apple says this generation represents the biggest jump in battery life iPhone history ever. So let’s break down what’s changed … more…
fullText:
Apple has just announced the new flagship iPhone lineup, featuring iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. One of the biggest improvements is battery life. 

In fact, Apple says this generation represents the biggest jump in battery life iPhone history ever. So let’s break down what’s changed … 

Apple says the boosts to battery life on the new iPhones is achieved through a combination of new physical internal battery designs, improved efficiency due to the new A20 Pro chip, and system software optimizations.

Obviously, real-world battery life will be put to the test when reviewers get their hands on the new iPhones. For now, we can go off the spec sheets which we can demonstrate the relative increases. 

Apple provides battery life stats in terms of hours of streaming video playback to compare with earlier models. 

iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone 17 Pro battery life

For reference, iPhone 17 Pro touts up to 30 hours streaming video playback and iPhone 17 Pro Max gets up to 35 hours streaming video playback. 

With iPhone 18 Pro, the claimed longevity is 33 hours streaming video playback. That’s a 10% improvement compared to iPhone 17 Pro.

For the Max size, battery life goes from 35 hours to a claimed 40 hours streaming video playback on iPhone 18 Pro Max. That’s an increase of about 14%. 

Apple also provided a new battery life metric for the 18 series that attempts to more closely represent real-world usage, than just video playback. This includes a variety of activities like messaging, taking photos, playing games, web browsing, and more, based on what it knows people actually use their iPhones for. 

On that benchmark, iPhone 18 Pro Max will apparently be able to last for 30 hours on a single charge. iPhone 18 Pro achieves 24 hours under the same conditions.

The above figures are based on the iPhone 18 Pro models with eSIM, such as those sold inside the United States. The models sold in many international markets still accommodate a physical SIM tray, which impinges on battery life a little: Apple says the non-eSIM versions get 2 hours less streaming video playback. 

iPhone Duo battery life

Obviously, a lot of attention today is on the shiny new iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone. The Duo actually incorporates two battery cells, one in each side of the device. But it also has to power two displays, including the inner 7.8-inch display that is the biggest ever in an iPhone by a significant margin.

However, its claimed battery life is still respectable. Apple claims users can expect 26 hours streaming video playback when using the large inner display, and up to 37 hours when using the outer display. Assuming heavy usage of the inner display, the Duo’s battery life is roughly equivalent to the iPhone 17 Pro — based on these published numbers.

We’ll know more exactly how the iPhone Duo fares in terms of all-day battery life when people start getting them in their hands. While the iPhone 18 Pro goes up for preorder this weekend, the Duo does not go on sale until October 23, so we’ve still got to wait a little bit for hands-on impressions.

title: watchOS 27 upgrade coming to Apple Watch this month
snippet: watchOS 27 is coming this month, and now we have an official release date. Apple says we can expect the Apple Watch software update on Monday, September 14. The Apple Watch software update brings Siri AI, new ways to launch apps, and more changes to the device. more…
fullText:
watchOS 27 is coming this month, and now we have an official release date. Apple says we can expect the Apple Watch software update on Monday, September 14. The Apple Watch software update brings Siri AI, new ways to launch apps, and more changes to the device.

Siri AI is the biggest addition, giving Apple Watch a dedicated Siri app and a more capable assistant for answering questions. Conversations also sync across supported Apple devices.

As I wrote last week, Siri AI had a rough summer in beta, but watchOS 27 beta 8 brought a major improvement in my testing. Everyday requests finally felt responsive again, while broader knowledge questions made the watch more useful without always requiring the iPhone.

However, watchOS 27 also removes some familiar features. Walkie-Talkie is gone, and double-clicking the Digital Crown no longer provides its previous multitasking shortcut.

Pressing the Digital Crown now opens a dynamic app grid with suggested apps and Siri. The full app launcher remains available, but takes another step to reach.

Other additions include a unified Find My app, expanded Smart Stack suggestions, and improvements to Workout Buddy.

watchOS 27 supports Apple Watch Series 9 and later, Apple Watch Ultra 2 and later, and Apple Watch SE 3.

Read more in our roundup of new watchOS 27 features.

title: Instagram’s latest feature lets you add tagged posts to your profile grid
snippet: Instagram's newest feature lets users take posts from the Tagged tab and move it to their main profile grid instead.
fullText:
Instagram is rolling out a small but useful new feature that gives users a little more control over what appears on their profiles. Starting today, you can add posts you’re tagged in directly to your main profile grid.

While it’s not exactly a groundbreaking update, it’s one of those changes that a lot of people will probably find useful. Most of us have experienced coming home from a party, concert, vacation, or night out with friends and going through the shared album, only to realize one of them has already beaten everyone to the punch and posted one of the best group photos, tagging you in the process.

While you could post the same photo yourself, that feels a little awkward. So Instagram now has a solution.

You can add a tagged post to your grid from the DM notification you receive when you’re tagged, directly from the post itself, or through your Tagged tab. If you change your mind later, you can easily remove the post from your profile.

The original post stays exactly where it is. Adding it to your grid doesn’t delete or duplicate the original post, and you can remove it from your profile at any time without removing it from your Tagged tab. 

Image Credits:Instagram

Instagram says the feature could also be useful for creator collaborations, giving creators another way to showcase posts they’ve been tagged in without having to republish the same content or use the “Invite collaborators” option. It could also come in handy for brand campaigns featuring multiple creators who want to highlight a piece of content they were all tagged in on their profiles.

The update is part of a broader push from Instagram to give users more control over how their profiles look. Back in June, Instagram introduced the “Reorder your grid” feature, allowing users to rearrange the content on their main profile grid. 

Instagram has also been adding new tools to make creating and managing content easier. One recent addition is “First Draft,” a new editing feature that automatically trims selected video clips and removes pauses, pulling together the best moments into an initial cut.

There’s also the newly launched “Replace Audio” tool, which lets users update the music on an existing post whenever they want.

title: Google is making it easier to switch between password managers on Android
snippet: Google's new feature will transfer your passkeys as well.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

9:00 AM PDT · September 10, 2026

Image Credits:Google

		

							

											
									

					

	

Google on Thursday introduced a new password manager switching experience on Android that doesn’t require you to download CSV files when migrating to a new app.

With the new feature, users will be able to move all of their passwords — and even passkeys — between apps seamlessly. 

To use the new system, users first open their new password manager app and choose to import or copy passwords from the old manager app. Android will detect manager apps on the device and coordinate transfer between both apps. Users can review the information being transferred and approve it in a few taps.

Image Credits:Google

Because this method also supports passkey transfer, users won’t need to set them up again when moving to a new password manager app. Plus, the company said that this averts the risk of exposing data from a CSV file.

Google said the new experience is already available on select partners as well as in Google’s own password manager app. Bitwarden, 1Password, and Dashlane are currently supported, with more apps coming in the future.

The password manager switching feature will be available on all devices running Android 8 or above.

title: No iPhone Ultra today? Three possible explanations …
snippet: It was widely expected that the first foldable iPhone set to be launched later today would be named the iPhone Ultra. However, a report yesterday said that the device will instead be called the iPhone Duo. If accurate, it’s an interesting development as it might potentially point to the company reserving the Ultra suffix for a completely different future model … more…
fullText:
It was widely expected that the first foldable iPhone set to be launched later today would be named the iPhone Ultra. However, a report yesterday said that the device will instead be called the iPhone Duo.

If accurate, it’s an interesting development as it might potentially point to the company reserving the Ultra suffix for a completely different future model … 

Opinion pieces in which I muse about possible future developments are by their very nature speculative, and this one perhaps more than most. When it comes to hard facts, the only thing we can say for sure is that Apple has used the Ultra label to mean the top-level offering in three contexts:

Apple Watch Ultra

Apple Silicon chips (eg. M5 Ultra)

CarPlay Ultra

It’s been speculated that the company plans to expand the use of the Ultra moniker to a range of new products. This was expected to include the iPhone Ultra and the MacBook Ultra.

Specifically, the iPhone Ultra label was reportedly going to be used for the foldable phone being launched later today. As of yesterday, however, we are expecting this to be named the iPhone Duo – so what’s up? I can see three possibilities.

1. The least interesting reason

The least interesting explanation would be that Apple isn’t using the Ultra label because the foldable phone isn’t the ultimate iPhone. It’s a device with a unique feature, but it’s expected to be inferior to the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max in several ways. If all the reports pan out, it won’t have a variable aperture lens on the main camera, and will also lack a telephoto camera; it won’t have Face ID; and it won’t match the battery life of the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

Logically then, it shouldn’t be called the iPhone Ultra. But Apple hasn’t always followed the logic when it comes to product names – for example, the MacBook Air weighing more than the 12-inch MacBook back in 2015, and the Mac Studio being more powerful than the Mac Pro in 2022. So while this is one possible explanation, it’s far from a definitive one.

2. The Ultra will be the 20th anniversary model

A related possibility is that the iPhone Ultra label is slated for the 20th anniversary model expected next year, taking a significant step closer to that long-term ‘single slab of glass’ vision. If that combined the slickest design with iPhone Pro capabilities, then that would indeed be worthy of the name.

3. There’s something even bigger in the works

The most exciting possibility is that Apple won’t be done with all-new additions to the iPhone range after the launch of the slab of glass (iPhone Glass?), and that the iPhone Ultra label is being reserved for a completely different model – one that really would sit at the top of the lineup in every respect.

I won’t get into speculation about what form that might take, though it will surprise nobody when I say my own hopes would center around significantly superior camera capabilities, starting with a much larger sensor. 

Where do you stand? Which of the three explanations do you think most likely? Or do you have a better idea of your own? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Hands-on: Honor’s Robot Phone is probably the coolest phone you still can’t buy
snippet: Decked out with a gimbal and shockingly good camera, the Robot Phone is one of the weirdest devices to come out of Honor. Even if you ignore the fact that it’s limited to China, Honor can’t keep up with demand. more…
fullText:
Decked out with a gimbal and shockingly good camera, the Robot Phone is one of the weirdest devices to come out of Honor. Even if you ignore the fact that it’s limited to China, Honor can’t keep up with demand.

When Honor began teasing a device that hid a fully functional gimbal and a 200MP camera tucked away in its camera bar, it truly seemed like an AI-driven fever dream of what future phones might look like.

Having played around with one this past week, I’m not distancing myself from that thought. Still, I can’t deny it’s a ridiculously cool idea, and a now fully functional Android phone the company launched last month.

Honor’s Robot Phone is aimed at creators more than anyone, for obvious reasons. The 200MP camera sits inside the device’s camera bar, which shouldn’t get you any weird looks if you use it in its retracted form. But as soon as you hit a certain dedicated camera app button and move the physical protective cover, that massive camera rises out of the Robot Phone’s rear panel as if it belonged in a horror movie.

	

The additional 50MP ultrawide and 200MP periscope camera do not move.

The camera app leaves controls up to the user, with full pan/tilt controls and a wide range to cover just about anything in view. It can be flipped 180 degrees for selfie capture, or used outward to record or capture the world in front of you.

Beyond that, Honor has packed some really cool film tools and recording formats. There are panning options and automatic spin controls to get neat shots you’d need to be really skilled to get with your regular old phone. The phone, being a product of Honor’s focus on AI, has object and person tracking. It works better than I anticipated during my short time with the phone, and stabilization was shockingly good for what is, again, a gimbal attached to a phone.

Its bag of tricks is huge, and it was a ton of fun to play around with. Honor pushes a little beyond simple camera tools with the AI-assisted mode, which is what some of the earliest teasers for the phone showcased. MagicOS has an AI assistant named “YOYO,” and it charges it with the ability to look around and gather digital information like a pair of smart glasses would.

It has its struggles when asking it questions in English instead of Chinese, but it’s a neat concept if a little unsettling.

Beyond the camera tools and mechanical gimbal, the Robot Phone brings many of the standard feature sets MagicOS 10 builds out for the manufacturer’s other devices. Overall, it’s a fun and interesting concept that deserves a ton of credit in what can often be a monotonous phone landscape.

At RMB 9,999 – nearly $1,500 – Honor’s Robot Phone is priced well, all things considered. That’s the running price for the 12/512GB configuration. The 16GB/1TB model nears $2,000.

But you probably couldn’t buy it if you wanted to. On top of being launched for the Chinese market with no global launch expected, Honor shared that the device reached sales targets almost immediately. It seemingly kept expectations low, and now has to catch up with demand while supplies are difficult to get a hand on for reasonable prices.

Again, I only messed around with the Robot Phone for a short time, but it ended up being one of those hands-on sessions that reminded me phones can be exceptionally fun. I’m not saying every phone should have an extending gimbal and overkill camera setup, but it’s kind of cool that the option exists – even if heavily limited.

title: Where Google Wallet state IDs are available on Android
snippet: States across the US are slowly rolling out support for adding your driver’s license or ID to the Google Wallet app on Android. more…
fullText:
States across the US are slowly rolling out support for adding your driver’s license or ID to the Google Wallet app on Android.

Update 9/5

How to add your state ID on Android

Open the Google Wallet app on Android 9+

Tap the “plus” button next to “View more” at the bottom

Choose “ID & personal info” and then “Driver’s license or state ID” 

Select your state and follow the instructions

The process involves taking a picture of the front and back of your physical card, as well as a short video of yourself for verification: a “photo from this video will be submitted to your ID issuer.” 

Once approved, the ID will appear below the carousel of payment methods alongside other passes. The order can be rearranged, while you can remotely remove the ID online if your phone is missing: myaccount.google.com > Personal Info > Manage IDs.

	

What Google Wallet state IDs are supported

Arizona (Rolled out October 2023)

Arkansas (Rolled out October 2025)

California (Rolled out August 2024)

Colorado (Rolled out October 2023)

Georgia (Rolled out October 2023)

Iowa (Rolled out June 2025)

Maryland (Rolled out December 2022)

Montana (Rolled out August 2025)

New Mexico (Rolled out December 2024)

North Dakota (Rolled out October 2025)

[New] Ohio (Rolled out September 2026)

Puerto Rico (Rolled out October 2025)

Where state IDs are coming next

Google previously said to expect support in the following places:

West Virginia (Upcoming availability announced April 2025)

Where you can use state IDs

The primary place you can use this digital ID is at TSA checkpoints in some US airports. There are two ways to do so, starting with tapping your phone at the NFC terminal. You then review the information that will be shared with the TSA and authenticate with device unlock. There’s also a QR code method that requires opening the ID in Google Wallet. 

Officially, you still have to carry the physical ID card at all times.

Some apps, like from car rental services, are beginning to accept digital IDs for identity and age verification. On mobile, if an app or website requests your age, it’s as simple as confirming (and authenticating) that you want to share this information with a system-level prompt/sheet. On desktop web, the experience involves scanning a QR code. 

Google wants to make it possible to do that “without any possibility to link back to a user’s personal identity” through what it calls Zero-Knowledge Proof. This technology will be open-sourced for anyone to use. 

Looking ahead, the IDs can be used at DMVs in Arizona, Georgia, Maryland, and New Mexico as part of “improved and streamlined customer experiences.”

	

Google is also working on letting you use digital IDs to “recover Amazon accounts, access online health services with CVS and MyChart by Epic, verify profiles on platforms like Uber and more.”

Using passport as REAL ID

Google in April pointed out how you can “use your ID pass created from a U.S. passport with TSA security for domestic travel at supported airports, even if you do not have a REAL ID driver’s license or state-issued ID.” This comes ahead of the May 7, 2025 deadline. 

To do so, open Google Wallet > Add to Wallet > ID pass. This three-step process involves taking a picture of your passport’s info page, and then scanning the security chip found inside the back cover of your passport. You also have to record a video of your face that Google will review “to make sure you’re a real person, and compare the video to your passport photo to make sure you’re the owner of the passport.”

The NFC and QR code instructions for using this digital passport ID are unchanged from above. You also have to keep the physical version on you when traveling. As a reminder, this won’t work internationally.

title: Honor Magic 9 Pro Max melds a classic ARRI camera with an iPhone-like look, launches this month
snippet: Honor has officially shown off its next flagship, the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max, which has a pretty familiar-looking design, a massive camera powered by ARRI, and a release date that’s mere weeks away. more…
fullText:
Honor has officially shown off its next flagship, the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max, which has a pretty familiar-looking design, a massive camera powered by ARRI, and a release date that’s mere weeks away.

Honor Magic 9 Pro Max is a new entry to the company’s flagship lineup, arriving on top of the Pro that was at the top of the list in prior years – “Pro Max” is a whole trend this year, it seems.

There’s still a ton we don’t know about this new device, but it’s clear that the camera is right at the center of the conversation.

A huge camera lens on the back takes up over half of the phone’s width, with two other cameras flanking it. They all sit on an iPhone-like camera island with an accent color on the bottom half of the device – this is a very obvious case of “inspiration” drawn from Apple’s latest, though Honor argues the arrangement “draws inspiration from the design language of one of ARRI’s most iconic cinema cameras.” 

	

Honor explains:

The design journey of the HONOR Magic9 Pro Max began with a simple question: How can a device inspire the same sense of creative possibility as cinema? For nearly a century, ARRI has helped filmmakers turn imagination into moving images. In 1937, the iconic ARRIFLEX cinema camera revolutionized professional filmmaking with its legendary “three-lens turret”—a design that brought function, precision, and industrial beauty into one form. Today, HONOR joins hands with ARRI to bring that timeless inspiration to the HONOR Magic9 Pro Max through an all-new camera architecture. (Image attached)

There’s clear inspiration in the camera design, but the phone as a whole certainly brings in some iPhone vibes, and it’s a wild change of pace from last year’s Honor Magic 8.

Specs on the cameras and the phone as a whole aren’t official yet, but ARRI is a part of the processing pipeline, just like on Honor’s Robot Phone. 

Hands-on: Honor’s Robot Phone is probably the coolest phone you still can’t buy

The signature color here is “Moss Green” and Honor says it will fully unveil the Magic 9 Pro Max on September 28. That’s only in China, though, with a global release presumably following later on.

title: Apple TV is about to kick off four weeks straight of big premieres
snippet: Apple TV has a strong fall lineup coming up, including four weeks straight of big premieres that kick off next week with critical hit Slow Horses. Here’s what’s coming. more…
fullText:
Apple TV has a strong fall lineup coming up, including four weeks straight of big premieres that kick off next week with critical hit Slow Horses. Here’s what’s coming.

September 16: Slow Horses (season 6)

Slow Horses continues its streak of debuting new seasons every year, and season 6 sounds like a standout winner per reviews.

This British espionage series based on Mick Herron’s novels returns with more dark humor, thrilling plot twists, and the beloved Slough House crew led by Gary Oldman’s Jackson Lamb.

Here’s Apple’s official series summary:

This darkly funny espionage drama follows a team of British intelligence agents who serve in a dumping ground department of MI5 due to their career-ending mistakes. Led by their brilliant but irascible leader, the notorious Jackson Lamb (Academy Award winner Sir Gary Oldman), they navigate the espionage world’s smoke and mirrors to defend England from sinister forces.

You can watch Slow Horses here on Apple TV.

September 23: Brothers

Brothers pairs stars and longtime friends Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson in a new comedy series with a fun premise.

The showrunner, Lee Eisenberg, is best known as writer and producer behind some of the best seasons of sitcom The Office.

Here’s the official series summary:

“Brothers” follows McConaughey and Harrelson, who play fictionalized versions of themselves, and whose lifelong friendship is thrown into chaos when they uncover a decades-old secret: they might actually be brothers. After Woody’s daughter’s wedding falls apart, he loads up the family and heads to Austin for an extended stay at Matthew’s ranch. But what begins as a healing getaway quickly spirals when Matthew’s mother, Ma Mac (played by Holland Taylor), accidentally lets slip a long-buried secret that the two friends might actually be brothers. As Woody turns the ranch upside down in pursuit of the truth, Matthew finds himself juggling an entirely different identity crisis: a potential run for Governor of Texas. The result is a heartfelt, chaotic and wildly funny story about friendship, family, fame and the messy line between myth and reality.

You can add Brothers to your Apple TV Watchlist here.

October 2: The Last First: Winter K2

The Last First: Winter K2 is a documentary exploring the high-risk practice of extreme mountain climbing.

The film has a 100% Rotten Tomatoes score, and many reviews highlight that it offers a unique angle that could surprise viewers. Per Variety: “The Last First is a revealing look at how they risked their lives for an ideal, maybe for an addiction. It’s a movie that shows us the dark side of literally getting high.”

Here is Apple’s official summary:

In “The Last First: Winter K2,” Amir Bar-Lev tells a complex, harrowing and moving story that takes an unflinching look at the industry of extreme mountain climbing and its changing culture. Focusing on a 2021 expedition, this documentary follows Icelander John Snorri Sigurjónsson and the Pakistani father-son team of Ali and Sajid Sadpara, a party of mountaineers who set out to be the first to summit K2 in the winter, when the mountain’s conditions are the cruelest. The men soon find themselves sharing the treacherous ascent with influencer climbers and their film crews, commercial expedition clients, and a Nepalese team no longer content to help Westerners achieve mountaineering glory. “The Last First: Winter K2” takes us to the icy heights and unpredictable weather of K2 and reveals a surprising and layered story — one of strategy and determination, class and caste, money and power — all under life-and-death circumstances.

You can add The Last First: Winter K2 to your Apple TV Watchlist here.

October 7 & 9: Small Prophets and Matchbox The Movie

Small Prophets arrives October 7 as a unique addition to Apple TV’s library. Unlike nearly every other show Apple offers for streaming, it’s not original to the service. Instead, Apple licensed the show after it became a hit in the UK earlier this year. It’s an award-winning comedy that viewers around the globe will soon get to enjoy for the first time.

Matchbox The Movie premieres October 9, a new action-comedy film inspired by the Mattel toys. It’s the kind of movie that feels very theatrical, with big stars and a big budget, but will premiere exclusively on Apple TV.

Here are Apple’s summaries for Small Prophets and Matchbox The Movie:

“Small Prophets” is a comic tale of the eccentric Michael Sleep (Pearce Quigley) who, since his darling Clea disappeared seven years ago, has lived a very ordinary life. He works in a DIY store, visits his dad Brian (Sir Michael Palin) and hopes for Clea to return. One day Brian shares an old recipe involving rainwater, horse manure and more than a little alchemy. With recipe in hand, Michael sets out (albeit with some skepticism) to create homunculi — magical spirits that can predict the future — in the hope they have the answer to his burning question: “will I ever see Clea again?”

“Matchbox The Movie” is an action-packed, globetrotting adventure about a group of friends since childhood who have their lives upended when undercover CIA agent Sean (John Cena), their long-absent former leader, returns to their small town and unwittingly gets them embroiled in a frantic international pursuit to save the world.

Add to your Apple TV Watchlist: Small Prophets and Matchbox The Movie.

fullText:
Those with very long memories might have spotted a resemblance between the iPhone Duo and a prototype device seen way back in 2009, the Microsoft Courier.

My headline is, of course, tongue-in-cheek: Microsoft never got any further than the prototype, and abandoned the project less than a year later. All the same, it is remarkable now to look back at it and see just how similar it is in terms of the integrated user-interface …

I said in my earlier piece that Apple has shown the world how to properly make a foldable smartphone, and that the clever integration between hardware and software is absolutely key to this.

One of the examples I gave was dragging part of a photo from one side of the screen to a separate app on the other, so it’s quite amusing to see Microsoft demonstrating a very similar capability in that 2009 concept video.

Microsoft did run with some of this type of capability with some of its Surface products, but it’s ironic that it took Apple to really match the level of integration the company originally had in mind. Check out the video below.

title: The Duo is drool-worthy, but the iPhone 18 Pro camera features win for me
snippet: If ever there was a head versus heart moment in terms of Apple tech, it was in yesterday’s unveiling of the new iPhones. I already started the morning by wiping the drool from my desk after watching the iPhone Duo sections of yesterday’s keynote, but the true hero of yesterday’s show for me was the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max, thanks to the new camera features … more…
fullText:
If ever there was a head versus heart moment in terms of Apple tech, it was in yesterday’s unveiling of the new iPhones.

I already started the morning by wiping the drool from my desk after watching the iPhone Duo sections of yesterday’s keynote, but the true hero of yesterday’s show for me was the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max, thanks to the new camera features … 

The variable aperture – with caveat

Given the supply chain needed to introduce a variable aperture lens to the iPhone, it was no surprise that this was well and truly leaked prior to the launch. The only thing that wasn’t completely clear is whether the feature would be included in both iPhone Pro models or just the Pro Max, and the good news is that the former applies.

Apple also confirmed that while the iPhone will vary the aperture automatically in some cases, we can also take full manual control. I said beforehand that we might need to temper our expectations of just how much difference the feature will make.

The main limiting factor of iPhones is not the lens aperture – which is already rather wide – but rather the size of the sensor. Again, all else being equal, the larger the sensor, the shallower DOF you’ll be able to achieve. Compared to DSLRs and mirrorless cameras, iPhones have absolutely tiny sensors, and that isn’t going to change this year. Given the same size sensor and a very slightly wider aperture, physics would suggest that we shouldn’t expect very much.

But I also speculated about whether Apple might have improved the Portrait mode capabilities in this latest model and actually be using a combination of the wider aperture and computational photography in order to deliver a more impressive result than would be obtained from the hardware alone. That remains to be seen, but based on some of the sample photos shown, I do suspect I may have been right about this.

I’ll be experimenting with this and will of course share the results.

Low-light photography and videography

The widest aperture is also close to one stop brighter – up from f/1.78 in the iPhone 17 Pro to f/1.48. While it may not make much difference to depth of field in itself, it should be a worthwhile improvement for low-light captures, including night shots.

Manual control of shutter speed

In addition to being able to manually control the aperture, we can also select the shutter speed for both still photos and video.

For still photos, that means the ability to take long exposure photos. The promotional video demonstrated using this to achieve motion blur. We don’t yet know the maximum exposure time possible, and whether a combination of the narrowest aperture and computational trickery will allow 30-second exposures, which are commonly used to make flowing water look silky smooth. The same technique can also be used to remove passers-by from a scene.

With conventional cameras, that requires a neutral density filter to cut down the amount of light, but there are third-party iPhone apps that can combine a whole series of photos into a single image to achieve a similar effect. I quite frequently use the Spectre app in this way.

For video, manual control of the shutter speed allows us to use the 180-degree rule. When shooting at 24 frames per second, we want the shutter speed set to 1/48th of a second to achieve the most natural-looking motion blur. This is something we can do in third-party pro camera apps like Blackmagic Cam, but it’s great to have the same capability in the stock Apple one.

White balance control

Another feature found in third-party apps is white balance control, and this too now comes to the stock app.

For still photography, this allows us to adjust the color temperature to our taste, but it’s most important in video footage. Automatic white balance means that the color temperature, and thus the whole look of the scene, can change during a clip. This creates a very visibly amateurish look. Being able to lock white balance for the duration of a clip is a huge improvement.

Cinematic mode for all video footage

Cinematic mode is the video equivalent of Portrait mode, allowing us to apply an artificial shallow depth of field effect. So far, we’ve always had to choose between shooting standard video and Cinematic mode footage – though the latter does actually give us a flat file also. The iPhone 18 Pro lets us decide afterwards to apply Cinematic mode effects to standard video footage.

Additionally, we can now shoot Cinematic video at up to 60 frames per second, allowing it to be used for slow motion footage. 

Smart focus mode for video

Existing iPhones already allow us to set the focus to track a particular person within a scene, but the iPhone 18 Pro introduces a significantly more advanced version of this.

In particular, it appears to use AI to identify a particular individual so that it can continue reliably tracking them even when somebody else passes between us and our subject. Additionally, it will re-lock on them if they leave the frame and re-enter it while shooting.

Histogram

This feature was reported ahead of yesterday’s keynote, so I’ll simply echo what I said then.

Judging exposure visually can be extremely unreliable, especially when viewing the iPhone screen in bright sunlight. Most dedicated cameras support a histogram feature intended to provide an accurate depiction of the exposure.

Battery life

Shooting video can burn through battery life, so an improvement here is welcome. We don’t know the specifics for this use, but since the maximum life of the Pro Max is up from 39 hours to 45 hours, that suggests we should expect to get around 15% more shooting time over last year’s model.

Apple Reference Image

Finally, there is a way to prove the authenticity of a photo should that be required. This is obviously a specialist tool most relevant to roles like photojournalism and law enforcement.

Wrap-up

Sure, some people are going to have eyes only for the iPhone Duo, and that’s perfectly understandable. But if your iPhone is an important part of your camera lineup, then the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are the champions here.
